claims.label: Reliance on chance variation and natural selection stalls inquiry into physical causes
claims.claim: As long as fortuitous variation and the survival of the fittest are accepted as sufficient explanations in biology, they will tend to hold back careful investigation of the real physical causes of organic form.
claims.quote: So long and so far as “fortuitous variation” and the “survival of the fittest” remain engrained as fundamental and satisfactory hypotheses in the philosophy of biology, so long will these “satisfactory and specious causes” tend to stay “severe and diligent inquiry,”
claims.scope: explanations of organic form in biology generally
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves and flowers are shaped by the laws of physics
claims.claim: The material parts of living things (cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves, flowers) are portions of matter whose particles have been moved, moulded and shaped in obedience to the laws of physics.
claims.quote: Cell and tissue, shell and bone, leaf and flower, are so many portions of matter, and it is in obedience to the laws of physics that their particles have been moved, moulded and conformed.
claims.scope: all organisms and their structural parts
measurable_quantities: mechanical stresses and surface tensions in tissues
claims.candidate_data: Cell and tissue shape imaging datasets (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) paired with published tissue mechanics measurements; 3D morphology scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Problems of organic form are mathematical and problems of growth are physical
claims.claim: The problems of the form of living things are, in the first instance, mathematical problems and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems, so morphology is a branch of physical science.
claims.quote: Their problems of form are in the first instance mathematical problems, and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems; and the morphologist is, _ipso facto_, a student of physical science.
claims.scope: morphology and the study of growth
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: No known physical law is transgressed by the bodily mechanism
claims.claim: However complex living processes are, no physical law (including those of chemistry, surface action and osmosis) is known to be broken by the working of the body.
claims.quote: But all the while, so far as I am aware, no physical law, any more than that of gravity itself, not even among the puzzles of chemical “stereometry,” or of physiological “surface-action” or “osmosis,” is known to be _transgressed_ by the bodily mechanism.
claims.scope: the physical and physiological mechanisms of all organisms
measurable_quantities: energy and mass balance of organisms
osmotic and surface forces in tissues
claims.candidate_data: Whole-organism calorimetry and energy-balance studies and published physiological measurements of osmosis and membrane transport.

claims.section: Form as a diagram of forces
claims.label: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it
claims.claim: The form of any portion of matter, living or dead, can be read as a diagram of forces: from the shape of a solid one can deduce the forces that produced and maintain it, and from the shape of a fluid the forces currently acting on it, so an organism's conformation is explained by a balance of forces.
claims.quote: In short, the form of an object is a “diagram of forces,” in this sense, at least, that from it we can judge of or deduce the forces that are acting or have acted upon it
claims.scope: living and non-living bodies, including whole organisms and cells
measurable_quantities: shape of cells or skeletal elements
measured or inferred mechanical stresses and forces
claims.candidate_data: Studies inferring cell and tissue forces from shape (cell-shape image datasets such as the Image Data Resource) and finite-element analyses of bone built on MorphoSource scans.

claims.label: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form
claims.claim: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.
claims.quote: Like other fluid bodies, its surface, whatsoever other substance, gas, liquid or solid, it be in contact with, and in varying degree according to the nature of that adjacent substance, is the seat of molecular force exhibiting itself as a surface-tension, from the action of which many important consequences follow, which greatly affect the form of the fluid surface.
claims.scope: fluid or semi-fluid cells such as Amoeba
claims.candidate_data: Published micropipette and atomic-force-microscopy measurements of cell cortical tension alongside cell-shape images (Image Data Resource).

claims.label: Protoplasm behaves as a highly viscous fluid that changes shape under force
claims.claim: The protoplasm of an Amoeba deforms and flows under the slightest pressure, so it is a fluid, but it is far more viscous than water, like treacle, and this viscosity slows its changes of shape.
claims.quote: While the protoplasm of the Amoeba reacts to the slightest pressure, and tends to “flow,” and while we therefore speak of it as a fluid, it is evidently far less mobile than such a fluid, for instance, as water, but is rather like treacle in its slow creeping movements as it changes its shape in response to force.
claims.scope: protoplasm of Amoeba and similar naked cells
claims.candidate_data: Published microrheology and micropipette-aspiration measurements of cytoplasmic viscosity in amoebae and other cells.

claims.label: Vital phenomena cannot be cleanly divided into physical and non-physical ones
claims.claim: There is no clear rule for deciding what is 'vital', and the properties of organisms cannot be clearly split into those of physical origin and those peculiar to living things, so physical analysis must proceed piece by piece.
claims.quote: it is plain that we have no clear rule or guide as to what is “vital” and what is not; the whole assemblage of so-called vital phenomena, or properties of the organism, cannot be clearly classified into those that are physical in origin and those that are _sui generis_ and peculiar to living things.
claims.scope: properties and processes of living organisms
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Nuclei, chromosomes and germ-plasm act only as seats of energy and centres of force
claims.claim: In development, variation and inheritance, material elements such as the spermatozoon, nucleus, chromosomes or germ-plasm never act as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and centres of force.
claims.quote: we must most carefully realise in the outset that the spermatozoon, the nucleus, the chromosomes or the germ-plasm can never _act_ as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and as centres of force.
claims.scope: embryology and heredity
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Changes in the length-weight constant k reveal changes of form during growth
claims.claim: Weight varies as the cube of length (W = kL³) in an animal of unchanging form and density, so tracking whether k stays constant or varies with length shows whether the animal's general form changes as it grows; such changes are likely as long as growth continues.
claims.notation: W = kL^3; form unchanged during growth \iff k constant
claims.quote: then the value of _k_, according to whether it varies or remains constant, will tell us at once whether there has or has not been a tendency to gradual alteration in the general form.
claims.scope: fishes and other growing animals of roughly constant density
claims.candidate_data: Length-weight relationship parameters compiled in FishBase and fisheries survey length-weight records.

claims.label: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height
claims.claim: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).
claims.notation: d \propto h^{3/2} (no buckling under own weight); h_{max} \approx 300\,\text{ft} for the Kew-flagstaff pine
claims.quote: In general, as Greenhill shews, the diameter of a homogeneous body must increase as the power 3/2 of the height, which accounts for the slender proportions of young trees, compared with the stunted appearance of old and large ones.
claims.scope: trees and other tall self-supporting plant stems
claims.candidate_data: Tree height-diameter allometry databases such as Tallo, national forest inventory data, and TRY plant traits for wood density and maximum height.

claims.label: Gravity sets an upper limit on the size of terrestrial animals
claims.claim: Because the strength of muscles and the crushing resistance of bones vary as their cross-section (the square of linear size) while body weight varies as the cube, there is a definite upper limit to the size of an animal living under gravity; the elephant, with disproportionately thick limb bones and reduced agility, is already near it.
claims.notation: strength \propto L^2, W \propto L^3 \Rightarrow strength/W \propto L^{-1}, so L is bounded above under gravity
claims.quote: But in a terrestrial animal the weight which tends to crush its limbs or which its muscles have to move, varies as the cube of its linear dimensions; and so, to the possible magnitude of an animal, living under the direct action of gravity, there is a definite limit set.
claims.scope: terrestrial animals, especially large mammals
claims.candidate_data: Published compilations of limb-bone circumference and body mass across mammals, 3D bone scans in MorphoSource, and body masses from PanTHERIA.

claims.label: Buoyancy removes the physical barrier to size in fully aquatic animals
claims.claim: An animal wholly immersed in water whose density about matches the water, like a whale, has its weight counterpoised, so there is no longer a physical barrier to its indefinite growth in size.
claims.quote: Under these circumstances there is no longer a physical barrier to the indefinite growth in magnitude of the animal.
claims.scope: fully aquatic animals of near-neutral buoyancy, e.g. whales
measurable_quantities: maximum body mass of aquatic versus terrestrial lineages
claims.candidate_data: Body-mass compilations for mammals (PanTHERIA) and fossil body-size records in the Paleobiology Database comparing aquatic and terrestrial maxima.

claims.label: Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly
claims.claim: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.
claims.notation: W_{muscle} \propto L^3; \dot{E}_{supply} \propto S \propto L^2
claims.quote: the singular result ought to follow that, in swimming for instance, the larger fish ought to be able to put on a spurt of speed far in excess of the smaller one; but the distance travelled by the year’s end should be very much alike for both of them.
claims.scope: similar, closely related animals of different size, especially swimming fish
claims.candidate_data: Published swimming-performance datasets (burst and critical swimming speeds), animal telemetry tracking records, and metabolic-rate data in AnAge and AnimalTraits.

claims.label: Power needed for flight grows as length^3.5 while muscle power grows as length^3
claims.claim: A bird of fixed proportions must fly at a minimum speed proportional to the square root of its linear size, so the work needed for flight varies as the 3½ power of linear size while the work its muscles can supply varies only as the cube; flight thus becomes harder as birds get larger (about 1.4 times harder per doubling of length).
claims.notation: V_{min} \propto L^{1/2}; W_{flight} = mV^2 \propto L^{7/2}; W_{muscle} \propto L^3; per doubling of L: 2^{7/2} : 2^3 \approx 1.4 : 1
claims.quote: The work requiring to be done, then, varies as the power 3½ of the bird’s linear dimensions, while the work of which the bird is capable depends on the mass of its muscles, and therefore varies as the cube of its linear dimensions.
claims.scope: flying birds of similar proportions
claims.candidate_data: Published bird flight-speed measurements (e.g. radar and tracking studies), flight-muscle mass compilations, and body masses from AnimalTraits.

claims.label: Ostrich and moa have passed the size at which muscular flight is possible
claims.claim: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.
claims.quote: It is not improbable that the ostrich has already reached a magnitude, and we may take it for certain that the moa did so, at which flight by muscular action, according to the normal anatomy of a bird, has become physiologically impossible.
claims.scope: large birds, including ratites
claims.candidate_data: Body-mass compilations of extant and extinct birds (AnimalTraits; Paleobiology Database for fossil taxa) with flight ability recorded.

claims.section: Giant fossil fliers and air density
claims.label: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere
claims.claim: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.
claims.quote: we have only to suppose that in carboniferous and jurassic days the terrestrial atmosphere was notably denser than it is at present, by reason, for instance, of its containing a much larger proportion of carbonic acid, and we have at once a means of reconciling the apparent mechanical discrepancy.
claims.scope: Carboniferous giant insects and Jurassic pterosaurs
measurable_quantities: reconstructed atmospheric density or composition through time
claims.candidate_data: Fossil insect and pterosaur size records in the Paleobiology Database and published geochemical reconstructions of Phanerozoic atmospheric CO2 and O2.

claims.label: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size
claims.claim: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.
claims.notation: impulse \propto M \Rightarrow v_0 independent of L; jump height h = v_0^2/2g independent of L
claims.quote: in other words, that all animals, provided always that they are similarly fashioned, with their various levers etc., in like proportion, ought to jump, not to the same relative, but to the same actual height.
claims.scope: jumping animals of similar construction across sizes, from fleas to horses
claims.candidate_data: Published comparative jumping-performance datasets across insects, frogs and mammals with body mass.

claims.label: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking
claims.claim: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.
claims.notation: V \propto L^{1/2} for swimming (Froude), flight (minimum speed) and walking (pendulum leg)
claims.quote: the general result, attained under very different conditions and arrived at by very different modes of reasoning, is in every case that the velocity tends to vary as the square root of the linear dimensions of the organism.
claims.scope: swimming, flying and walking animals of similar construction
claims.candidate_data: Published compilations of maximum and preferred locomotor speeds against body size for fish, birds and mammals, with body sizes from AnimalTraits or PanTHERIA.

claims.label: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like
claims.claim: The form and actions of terrestrial animals are conditioned by the strength of gravity: if it were doubled, bipedal form would fail and most land animals would resemble short-legged saurians or serpents; if halved, animals would be lighter, more active and need less heart, lungs and blood.
claims.quote: Were the force of gravity to be doubled, our bipedal form would be a failure, and the majority of terrestrial animals would resemble short-legged saurians, or else serpents.
claims.scope: terrestrial animals
measurable_quantities: skeletal and cardiovascular measures under altered gravity
claims.candidate_data: Published hypergravity centrifuge and spaceflight studies of animal morphology and physiology.

claims.label: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass
claims.claim: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.
claims.notation: S/M \approx \text{const} maintained by change of form, against S/M \propto L^{-1} for similar forms
claims.quote: Throughout the whole field of morphology we may find examples of a tendency (referable doubtless in each case to some definite physical cause) for surface to keep pace with volume, through some alteration of its form.
claims.scope: internal surfaces of animals, e.g. gut lining and brain cortex
measurable_quantities: cortical surface area or gyrification index
claims.candidate_data: Published comparative datasets of brain gyrification and cortical surface area across mammals and of intestinal surface area against body mass.

claims.label: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres
claims.claim: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.
claims.quote: In like manner we shall find that the form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity, and largely if not mainly due to the force of surface-tension
claims.scope: small organisms and individual cells versus large animals
measurable_quantities: shape sphericity or other shape descriptors
claims.candidate_data: Plankton and protist imaging datasets with size and shape measurements, and cell-shape data in the Image Data Resource.

claims.label: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones
claims.claim: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.
claims.quote: But it is by no means true that form and growth are in this direct and simple fashion correlative or complementary in the case of minute portions of living matter.
claims.scope: large multicellular organisms versus small organisms and individual cells
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse growth and morphometric datasets of developing organisms and of single cells (Image Data Resource).

claims.label: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass
claims.claim: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.
claims.notation: cell division keeps S/M \approx \text{const}; cleavage increases S at constant V and M
claims.quote: In short, however it may be brought about, the phenomenon of division of the cell will be precisely what is required to keep approximately constant the ratio between surface and mass, and to restore the balance between the surface-energy and the other energies of the system.
claims.scope: dividing cells, including cleaving eggs
claims.candidate_data: Cell-size and cell-cycle imaging datasets (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) and published embryo cleavage volume measurements.

claims.label: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size
claims.claim: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.
claims.quote: An immediate and remarkable result of the principles just described is a tendency on the part of all cells, according to their kind, to vary but little about a certain mean size, and to have, in fact, certain absolute limitations of magnitude.
claims.scope: tissue cells of animals, compared across individuals of different body size
claims.candidate_data: Published cell-size measurements across body sizes within and between species, and tissue histology images in the Image Data Resource.

claims.label: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells
claims.claim: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.
claims.quote: we may (with Enriques) lay it down as a general law that among animals, whether large or small, the ganglion-cells vary in size within narrow limits; and that, amidst all the great variety of structural type of ganglion observed in different classes of animals, it is always found that the smaller species have simpler ganglia than the larger, that is to say ganglia containing a smaller number of cellular elements.
claims.scope: nerve cells and ganglia across animal species
measurable_quantities: neuron number per ganglion or brain region
claims.candidate_data: Published comparative neuron-count datasets (isotropic fractionator studies across mammals and birds) and NeuroMorpho.Org neuron morphologies.

claims.label: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller
claims.claim: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.
claims.quote: it will still be clear that the smallest known bodies which are described as organisms draw nigh towards molecular magnitudes, and we must recognise that the subdivision of the organism cannot proceed to an indefinite extent, and in all probability cannot go very much further than it appears to have done in these already discovered forms.
claims.scope: the smallest micro-organisms
measurable_quantities: number of protein molecules per cell
claims.candidate_data: Published cell-size measurements of the smallest bacteria and archaea, and proteomic estimates of protein copy number per cell.

claims.section: Form as a function of growth rates
claims.label: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions
claims.claim: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.
claims.quote: It is the ratio between the rates of growth in various directions by which we must account for the external forms of all, save certain very minute, organisms.
claims.scope: all organisms except very minute ones (e.g. single small cells shaped by surface tension)
measurable_quantities: directional growth rates (length, breadth, depth per unit time)
claims.candidate_data: Longitudinal morphometric growth series and 3D developmental image time-lapses (e.g. published ontogenetic shape datasets on Dryad, MorphoSource specimen series).

claims.section: Form as a function of growth rates
claims.label: Constant growth-rate ratios preserve form; changing ratios produce development
claims.claim: When the ratio between growth rates in different directions stays constant, an organism grows in bulk with little or no change of form; such constancy seldom lasts more than a season, and when the ratio alters the organism undergoes development, a steady and persistent change of form.
claims.quote: It may sometimes be a very _constant_ one, in which case the organism, while growing in bulk, suffers little or no perceptible change in form; but such equilibrium seldom endures for more than a season, and when the _ratio_ tends to alter, then we have the phenomenon of morphological “development,” or steady and persistent change of form.
claims.scope: growing multicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: ratios of linear dimensions over age
rate of change of shape indices
claims.candidate_data: Longitudinal growth and shape datasets for animals and plants (e.g. ontogenetic morphometric series on Dryad, human growth cohort data).

claims.label: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet
claims.claim: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.
claims.quote: the various foldings of the blastoderm, by which the neural and amniotic folds were brought into being, were essentially and obviously the resultant of unequal rates of growth,—of local accelerations or retardations of growth,—in what to begin with was an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue.
claims.scope: vertebrate embryos (blastoderm / germinal disc), especially the chick
measurable_quantities: local tissue growth rates (cell proliferation, area expansion)
claims.candidate_data: Live-imaging and cell-tracking datasets of chick and other vertebrate embryos during neurulation (e.g. Image Data Resource entries, published tissue-growth maps).

claims.label: Differences between related forms emerge gradually and are small in the young
claims.claim: Because form differences are attained by growth at specific velocities over long periods, differences between any two related individuals or species must appear gradually and be little apparent in the young, and animals of very different adult size differ less and less in size and form when traced back through foetal stages.
claims.quote: it is accordingly obvious that in any two related individuals (whether specifically identical or not) the differences between them must manifest themselves gradually, and be but little apparent in the young. It is for the same simple reason that animals which are of very different sizes when adult, differ less and less in size (as well as in form) as we trace them backwards through the foetal stages.
claims.scope: related individuals and species, especially mammals with foetal development
measurable_quantities: size and shape divergence between species across developmental stages
foetal body size by gestational age across species
claims.candidate_data: Comparative embryo and foetal growth series and ontogenetic morphometric datasets (e.g. MorphoSource embryo scans, published comparative prenatal growth data).

claims.label: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens
claims.claim: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.
claims.quote: The curve of growth for length or stature in man indicates a rapid increase at the outset, that is to say during the quick growth of babyhood; a long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood; as a rule a marked quickening soon after the boy is in his teens, when he comes to “the growing age”
claims.scope: humans, birth to adulthood
claims.candidate_data: WHO and CDC growth reference data and national longitudinal growth cohort datasets.

claims.label: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age
claims.claim: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.
claims.quote: We should see that a man’s full stature endures but for a spell; long before fifty it has begun to abate, by sixty it is notably lessened, in extreme old age the old man’s frame is shrunken and it is but a memory that “he once was tall.”
claims.scope: adult humans
claims.candidate_data: Longitudinal ageing cohorts with repeated height measurement (e.g. Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, NHANES cross-sectional data).

claims.label: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth
claims.claim: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.
claims.notation: W \propto L^3 whatever the law of growth L(t)
claims.quote: whatever be the law of increment in a linear dimension, the law of increase in volume, and therefore in weight, will be that these latter magnitudes tend to vary as the cubes of the linear dimensions.
claims.scope: growing humans (and organisms generally)
claims.candidate_data: WHO/CDC growth references and longitudinal cohort data giving paired height and weight by age.

claims.label: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
claims.claim: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.
claims.quote: In short, throughout all this period, it is a very _similar_ curve in the two sexes; but it has its notable differences, in amplitude and especially in _phase_.
claims.scope: humans, childhood and adolescence
measurable_quantities: annual weight and height increments by age and sex
claims.candidate_data: Sex-specific growth velocity references (WHO, CDC) and longitudinal cohort datasets.

claims.label: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown
claims.claim: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.
claims.quote: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.
claims.scope: animals generally
claims.candidate_data: Comparative growth-curve compilations (e.g. AnAge, published vertebrate growth-curve datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
claims.claim: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.
claims.quote: But especially in the cold-blooded animals, such as fishes, the slowing-down period is very greatly protracted, and the size of the creature would seem never actually to reach, but only to approach asymptotically, to a maximal limit.
claims.scope: cold-blooded animals, especially fishes
claims.candidate_data: Fish length-at-age and growth-parameter compilations (e.g. FishBase growth data) and reptile growth records in AnAge.

claims.label: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
claims.claim: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).
claims.quote: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.
claims.scope: animals, especially mammals
measurable_quantities: age at cessation of growth or maturity
claims.candidate_data: Species-level life-history and growth databases (AnAge, PanTHERIA, AnimalTraits).

claims.label: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth
claims.claim: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.
claims.quote: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.
claims.scope: human foetus
claims.candidate_data: Foetal growth standards from ultrasound studies (e.g. INTERGROWTH-21st foetal growth data, WHO foetal growth charts).

claims.label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
claims.claim: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
claims.quote: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
claims.scope: humans, childhood and adolescence
measurable_quantities: coefficient of variation of stature and weight by age
claims.candidate_data: Growth reference datasets reporting age-specific standard deviations (WHO, CDC, national growth surveys).

claims.label: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis
claims.claim: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.
claims.quote: Just as the human curve of growth has its slight but well-marked interruptions, or variations in rate, coinciding with such epochs as birth and puberty, so is it with other animals, and this phenomenon is particularly striking in the case of animals which undergo a regular metamorphosis.
claims.scope: animals, including man, mouse, silkworm, tadpole
measurable_quantities: growth velocity around birth, weaning, puberty, moults and metamorphosis
claims.candidate_data: Longitudinal growth records of laboratory animals and insects (e.g. published mouse growth curves from the Mouse Phenome Database, insect larval growth datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Metamorphosis is often, perhaps always, accompanied by loss of bulk and weight
claims.claim: Negative growth, an actual loss of bulk and weight, often and perhaps always accompanies metamorphosis, as in the eel, the silkworm before pupation and the frog tadpole.
claims.quote: The negative growth, or actual loss of bulk and weight which often, and perhaps always, accompanies metamorphosis, is well shewn in the case of the eel.
claims.scope: animals with metamorphosis (insects, amphibians, eels)
measurable_quantities: body mass and dimensions before and after metamorphosis
claims.candidate_data: Published larval-to-juvenile body-size datasets for amphibians, insects and anguillid eels (e.g. Dryad metamorphosis size datasets).

claims.label: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain
claims.claim: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.
claims.quote: It is plain, then, that there is no simple and direct relation, holding good _throughout life_, between the size of the body as a whole and that of the organs we have just discussed; and the changing ratio of magnitude is especially marked in the case of the brain
claims.scope: humans and other vertebrates (lion, dogfish)
claims.candidate_data: Autopsy organ-weight reference datasets by age and comparative ontogenetic organ-mass data.

claims.label: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
claims.claim: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.
claims.notation: k = W/L^3 not constant in plaice; \max_L k at L \approx 30\,\text{cm}
claims.quote: we see that _k_ is by no means constant, but steadily increases to a maximum, and afterwards slowly declines with the increasing size of the fish
claims.scope: plaice (and by extension other fishes)
claims.candidate_data: Fisheries survey length-weight records and maturity data (e.g. ICES DATRAS survey data, FishBase length-weight relationships).

claims.label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
claims.claim: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
claims.quote: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.
claims.scope: plaice and similar seasonally spawning fishes
measurable_quantities: weight at fixed length by month
claims.candidate_data: Monthly fisheries sampling of length, weight and maturity stage (e.g. ICES survey and market-sampling data).

claims.section: Form as a function of growth rates
claims.label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
claims.claim: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.
claims.quote: a very large part of the specific morphology of the organism depends upon the fact that there is not only an average, or aggregate, rate of growth common to the whole, but also a variation of rate in different parts of the organism, tending towards a specific rate characteristic of each different part or organ.
claims.scope: multicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: body proportions across species and ontogeny
claims.candidate_data: Ontogenetic organ and limb growth datasets and comparative morphometrics (e.g. MorphoSource, Phenoscape, published relative-growth data on Dryad).

claims.label: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C
claims.claim: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.
claims.quote: this optimum temperature is very much the same for all the common plants of our own climate which have as yet been studied; in them it is somewhere about 26° C. (or say 77° F.), or about the temperature of a warm summer’s day
claims.scope: temperate and warm-climate plants (root and shoot elongation)
claims.candidate_data: Plant thermal response compilations and TRY plant traits database entries on temperature optima.

claims.label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction
claims.claim: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).
claims.notation: v(\theta + n) = x^n v(\theta) for a rise of n degrees; temperature coefficient of growth x^{10} \approx 2\text{--}3
claims.quote: Van’t Hoff’s law, which has become a fundamental principle of chemical mechanics, is likewise applicable (with certain qualifications) to the phenomena of vital chemistry; and it follows that, on very much the same lines, we may speak of the “temperature coefficient” of growth.
claims.scope: growth and development of plants and animals within normal temperature limits
measurable_quantities: growth or development rate at different temperatures
claims.candidate_data: Compilations of thermal performance and development-rate data for ectotherms and plants (e.g. published Q10 and thermal performance curve datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage
claims.claim: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.
claims.quote: It would seem to be this double effect of temperature in the case of the organism which gives us our “optimum” curves, which are the expression, accordingly, not of a primary phenomenon, but of a more or less complex resultant.
claims.scope: physiological processes, especially growth, in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: growth rate versus exposure duration at high temperature
claims.candidate_data: Thermal performance curve datasets with time-dependent exposure for plants and ectotherms (e.g. published thermal tolerance datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve
claims.claim: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
claims.notation: L(t) = \bar{L}(t) + A(t)\sin(2\pi t / 1\,\text{yr}), A(t) \to 0 as d\bar{L}/dt \to 0 (damped sine)
claims.quote: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.
claims.scope: fishes (plaice, haddock) and humans
claims.candidate_data: Fish otolith and scale increment datasets and human seasonal growth studies with sub-annual measurement.

claims.label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
claims.claim: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
claims.quote: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
claims.scope: Arizona climate, 1390s–1910s, inferred from ponderosa (yellow) pine rings
claims.candidate_data: International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB) ponderosa pine chronologies from Arizona and Southwest drought reconstructions (e.g. North American Drought Atlas).

claims.label: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism
claims.claim: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.
claims.quote: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells
claims.scope: growing cells of plants and animals, especially plant elongation and early embryos
claims.candidate_data: Plant cell expansion and turgor measurement studies and embryo water-content time series (published datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
claims.claim: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
claims.quote: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.
claims.scope: brine-shrimps (Artemia) in waters of varying salinity
claims.candidate_data: Artemia morphometric studies across salinity gradients and rearing experiments (published datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis
claims.claim: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.
claims.quote: it is sufficiently clear that the normal “curve of growth” of an organism, in all its general features, very closely resembles the velocity-curve of chemical autocatalysis.
claims.scope: growth of organisms generally
claims.candidate_data: Growth-curve datasets fitted with logistic and related models (e.g. published animal and plant growth curves on Dryad, AnAge).

claims.label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions
claims.claim: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
claims.quote: We may take it, then, as an established fact, whose full extent and bearings are still awaiting investigation, that there exist substances both within and without the organism which have a marvellous power of accelerating growth, and of doing so in such a way as to affect not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
claims.scope: animals (tadpoles, mammals, birds), with parallels in plants
measurable_quantities: growth rates of specific organs under hormone treatment
claims.candidate_data: Experimental endocrinology datasets on thyroid hormone in amphibian metamorphosis and growth hormone effects on body proportions (published studies on Dryad).

claims.label: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them
claims.claim: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.
claims.quote: And we then, I think, draw near to the conclusion that what is true of these is universally true, and that the great function of natural selection is not to originate, but to remove
claims.scope: evolution of organic form generally
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time
claims.claim: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.
claims.notation: V^m T^n = \text{const}; for regenerating tadpole tails V T^2 \approx \text{const}
claims.quote: And in this particular case, the equation _V_ _T_^2 = constant, holds very nearly true; that is to say the velocity varies, or tends to vary, inversely as the square of the time.
claims.scope: regenerating tadpole tails, possibly regeneration generally
measurable_quantities: regenerated length versus days after amputation
claims.candidate_data: Time-course regeneration measurements in amphibian larvae and zebrafish fins (published datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Regeneration is ordinary growth, with the same curve as growth from zero
claims.claim: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.
claims.quote: A complete curve of growth, starting from zero, has the same essential characteristics as the regeneration curve.
claims.scope: regenerating tissues and whole-organism growth
measurable_quantities: embryonic growth velocity versus time from conception
claims.candidate_data: Regeneration time-course data (amphibians, zebrafish) alongside prenatal growth curves (published datasets on Dryad).

claims.label: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates
claims.claim: Whether an amputated large crustacean claw regenerates as the large claw, or the claws exchange roles, depends on the ratio between the regenerative growth rate of the amputated claw and the growth rate of the uninjured claw, since claw form follows claw size.
claims.quote: It depends upon the respective rates of growth, upon a ratio between the rate of regeneration and the rate of growth of the uninjured limb
claims.scope: Crustacea with asymmetric claws (lobster, Alpheus, crabs)
measurable_quantities: claw size and form over successive moults
claims.candidate_data: Snapping shrimp and crab claw-regeneration experiment data (published studies on Dryad).

claims.label: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration
claims.claim: Reproduction by fission in worm-like animals consists essentially of the physical tendency of a long semi-fluid tube to break into segments, combined with ordinary regeneration, which explains its occurrence in zoologically unrelated animals and its absence in some close relatives.
claims.quote: If we add to this natural tendency towards fission of a cylindrical or tubular worm, the ordinary phenomenon of regeneration, we have all that is essentially implied in “reproduction by fission.”
claims.scope: worms and worm-like animals that reproduce by fission
claims.candidate_data: Phylogenetic trait data on asexual fission in annelids and flatworms combined with body-size data (e.g. published comparative datasets).

claims.label: Growth velocity peaks and falls because surface resistance suddenly increases
claims.claim: The abrupt change from increasing to decreasing growth velocity is more likely due to a sudden increase of resistance, such as the formation of a comparatively firm skin during histological differentiation, than to a decline of internal growth forces; the later slowing reflects waning growth forces against rising superficial resistance.
claims.quote: I take it that the sudden arrest of velocity is much more likely to be due to a sudden increase of resistance than to a sudden diminution of internal energies: in other words, I suspect that it is coincident with some notable event of histological differentiation, such as the rapid formation of a comparatively firm skin
claims.scope: growing organisms generally, including regenerating tissues
measurable_quantities: timing of skin or tissue differentiation
claims.candidate_data: Developmental tissue-mechanics measurements paired with growth time series (published embryo mechanics datasets).

claims.label: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history
claims.claim: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.
claims.quote: From one form, or ratio of magnitude, to another there is but one straight and direct road of transformation, be the journey taken fast or slow; and if the transformation take place at all, it will in all likelihood proceed in the self-same way, whether it occur within the life-time of an individual or during the long ancestral history of a race.
claims.scope: ontogeny and phylogeny of organic form
claims.candidate_data: Geometric morphometric datasets with ontogenetic and phylogenetic series (e.g. MorphoSource, Paleobiology Database occurrence and size data).

claims.label: Cell structure matters only as the visible expression of forces and energy
claims.claim: The study of visible cell structure has little value except as part of a dynamical investigation, because the activities of a cell are due to energy and forces, not to particular material particles or structures as such.
claims.quote: In short it would seem evident that, except in relation to a dynamical investigation, the mere study of cell structure has but little value of its own.
claims.scope: cells generally, including germ-cells and ova
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Spindle and asters as lines of force
claims.label: Mitotic figures require a polarised force like magnetism, not mechanical traction
claims.claim: The spindle and asters of dividing cells are lines of force of a bipolar field made visible by more permeable particles, like iron filings between magnet poles, and they cannot be explained by mere mechanical traction on a protoplasmic web but require some polarised and polarising force analogous to magnetism or electricity.
claims.quote: any explanation which is based, like Rhumbler’s, on mere mechanical traction, is obviously inadequate, and we shall find ourselves limited to the hypothesis of some polarised and polarising force, such as we deal with, for instance, in the phenomena of magnetism or electricity.
claims.scope: caryokinetic (mitotic) division of animal and plant cells
measurable_quantities: forces on chromosomes and spindle poles
claims.candidate_data: Published spindle mechanics and microtubule imaging studies (Image Data Resource mitotic screens such as MitoCheck) bear on the mechanism.

claims.label: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension
claims.claim: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells) the pressure becomes unsymmetrical and the nucleus is deformed.
claims.quote: So long as the fluid substance of the nucleus is qualitatively different from, and incapable of mixing with, the fluid or semi-fluid protoplasm which surrounds it, we shall expect it to be, as it almost always is, of spherical form.
claims.scope: nuclei of cells generally; contrasted with muscle and epithelial cells with stiffened cytoplasm
claims.candidate_data: Single-cell 3D imaging with segmented nuclear shapes (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) combined with published cytoplasmic and nuclear mechanics measurements.

claims.label: Morphological polarity of the cell is the outward sign of a dynamical polarity
claims.claim: The visible polarity of a cell (symmetry of structure about an axis, such as nucleus–centrosome or free–attached surface) is the outward expression of a real polarised distribution of forces, whose lines of force are made visible where particles of matter become strung together under those forces.
claims.quote: The _morphological_ “polarity” is accompanied by, and is but the outward expression (or part of it) of a true _dynamical_ polarity, or distribution of forces; and the “lines of force” are rendered visible by concatenation of particles of matter, such as come under the influence of the forces in action.
claims.scope: cells with recognisable axes of symmetry, e.g. ova, columnar and ciliated epithelial cells
measurable_quantities: orientation of granule or fibril alignment
claims.candidate_data: Imaging datasets of polarised epithelial cells (Image Data Resource) and published intracellular force or electric-field measurements.

claims.label: The alveolar meshwork of nucleus and cytoplasm is a surface-tension froth
claims.claim: The alveolar 'reticulum' seen in the nucleus and cytoplasm is a froth or foam produced by the interacting surface tensions of two intermixed fluids of similar density striving to separate, and is not inherent in the nature of protoplasm.
claims.quote: This phenomenon is nothing else than what we call in ordinary language, a “froth” or a “foam.” It is a surface-tension phenomenon, due to the interacting surface-tensions of two intermixed fluids, not very different in density, as they strive to separate.
claims.scope: nuclear and cytoplasmic alveolar meshworks of cells
claims.candidate_data: Live-cell and electron-microscopy image collections (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR) and published measurements of cytoplasmic phase separation.

claims.label: Fine internal networks and granules seen in fixed cells are largely artefacts
claims.claim: Fixation preserves the general outward form of small organisms and cells, but the minute internal networks and granules described as the structure of protoplasm are to a large extent artefacts of coagulating fixatives, although larger structures such as nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and the spindle are really present in the living cell.
claims.quote: While this assumption is reasonable and justified as regards the general outward form of small organisms or of individual cells, enough has been done of late years to shew that the case is totally different in the case of the minute internal networks, granules, etc., which represent the alleged _structure_ of protoplasm.
claims.scope: histological preparations of cells fixed with chemical reagents
measurable_quantities: presence and morphology of intracellular networks in living versus fixed cells
variation of fixed structure with fixative used
claims.candidate_data: Paired live-cell and fixed-cell imaging studies and cryo-electron tomography datasets (EMPIAR) comparing preserved structure.

claims.section: Nucleus and chromatin in the field
claims.label: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane
claims.claim: In the bipolar field between the centrosomes the nucleus as a whole behaves as a body more permeable than the cytoplasm and is drawn in between the poles, whereas its chromatin, once broken up, behaves like a diamagnetic body, is repelled to the weaker parts of the field, and so collects in a peripheral circle on the equatorial plane.
claims.quote: the fact is that the chromatin substance now _behaves_ after the fashion of a “diamagnetic” body, and is repelled from the stronger to the weaker parts of the field.
claims.scope: nuclei and chromosomes of dividing cells
measurable_quantities: chromosome position relative to spindle poles over time
chromosome distribution on the metaphase plate
claims.candidate_data: Live-cell time-lapse mitosis imaging datasets (Image Data Resource, Cell Tracking Challenge) give chromosome trajectories.

claims.label: Differences of electric potential play a great part in cell division
claims.claim: Differences of electric potential between cell constituents, and between parts of the egg, play a great part in cell division; the potential difference between animal and vegetative poles of a fertilised egg fluctuates or reverses at successive segmentations, and the electrical difference of chromatin is greatest at mitosis.
claims.quote: Among other investigations, all leading towards the same general conclusion, namely that differences of electric potential play a great part in the phenomenon of cell division
claims.scope: dividing cells and fertilised eggs (e.g. Fundulus, toad, turtle)
measurable_quantities: timing of potential reversals relative to cleavage
electrophoretic mobility of nuclei and cytoplasm
claims.candidate_data: Published bioelectric measurements in eggs and embryos (vibrating-probe and voltage-dye studies) deposited in supplementary data or Dryad.

claims.label: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces
claims.claim: In all cells the mechanical process of division must be explained as the result of a conflict between surface tension and its opposing forces, the division plane being set in the equatorial plane of the polar field.
claims.quote: in all cells whatsoever, the process of division must somehow be explained as the result of a conflict between surface-tension and its opposing forces.
claims.scope: all dividing cells
measurable_quantities: cortical tension at equator and poles during cytokinesis
orientation of cleavage plane relative to spindle axis
claims.candidate_data: Published micropipette aspiration and cortical tension measurements during cytokinesis, and mitosis imaging datasets in the Image Data Resource.

claims.label: Entry of the first spermatozoon raises the surface tension of the egg
claims.claim: Because later spermatozoa fail to enter the egg after the first, an immediate consequence of sperm entry is an increase in the surface tension of the egg.
claims.quote: other spermatozoa, subsequent to the first, fail to effect an entry, we may safely conclude that an immediate consequence of the entry of the spermatozoon is an increase in the surface-tension of the egg
claims.scope: fertilisation of animal eggs
measurable_quantities: egg surface tension or cortical tension before and after sperm entry
claims.candidate_data: Published measurements of egg cortical stiffness and polyspermy block in sea urchin, frog and mouse eggs.

claims.label: The pronuclei travel curved paths and meet before reaching the centre of the egg
claims.claim: Given an attraction between the male and female pronuclei and a force drawing them toward the egg centre, their paths lie within the triangle formed by the two bodies and the centre, are curved (convex toward the line joining them) unless they start on a diameter, and the pronuclei meet a little before the centre and then travel straight to it.
claims.quote: (2) unless the two bodies happen to lie, to begin with, precisely on a diameter of the cell, their paths until they meet one another will be curved paths, the convexity of the curve being towards the straight line joining the two bodies; (3) the two bodies will meet a little before they reach the centre;
claims.scope: pronuclear migration in fertilised eggs (e.g. frog)
measurable_quantities: 3D trajectories of male and female pronuclei
position of pronuclear meeting relative to egg centre
claims.candidate_data: Live 3D time-lapse imaging of pronuclear migration in sea urchin, C. elegans or mouse zygotes (Image Data Resource and published supplementary data).

claims.label: Mitotic phenomena follow from simple physical assumptions and have secondary significance
claims.claim: Most if not all of the intracellular phenomena of mitosis follow inevitably from very simple assumptions about the physical constitution of the cell and a simple distribution of polarised forces within it, and are likely to prove of only remote and secondary biological significance.
claims.quote: Most, if not all of them, would seem to follow immediately and inevitably from very simple assumptions as to the physical constitution of the cell, and from an extremely simple distribution of polarised forces within it.
claims.scope: intracellular phenomena of cell division in plants and animals
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen
claims.claim: Although chromosome number is constant within a species, the range of numbers across plants and animals is small: few organisms have fewer than six chromosomes in the germ-nuclei and fewer still have more than sixteen.
claims.quote: (as regards the germ-nuclei) few organisms have less than six chromosomes, and fewer still have more than sixteen
claims.scope: germ-nuclei (haploid chromosome number) of plants and animals
claims.candidate_data: Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB) for plants and published animal karyotype compilations.

claims.label: Details of mitosis vary among close relatives and are not specific to the organism
claims.claim: The details of mitosis (presence of visible caryokinesis, position of the field of force, number of chromosome groups, chromosome form and arrangement) vary greatly even among closely related organisms or within one species, and are not specifically related to the organism in which they occur.
claims.quote: there seem to be strong grounds for believing that these and many similar phenomena are in no way specifically related to the particular organism in which they have been observed, and are not even specially and indisputably connected with the organism as such.
claims.scope: mitosis in plants and animals, e.g. Copepods, Ascaris megalocephala
measurable_quantities: mitotic mode (open or closed, centrosomal or acentrosomal)
claims.candidate_data: Comparative cytology compilations of mitotic types across eukaryotes combined with phylogenies from the Open Tree of Life.

claims.label: Early embryological categories seldom coincide with phylogenetic classification
claims.claim: Early embryological data, up to and well beyond segmentation, are a subject for physiological and physical investigation, and their categories (yolk content, chromosome form and number, radial, bilateral or spiral cleavage) will only seldom and accidentally coincide with the natural or phylogenetic classification of the systematist.
claims.quote: But we have little right to expect, and in point of fact we shall very seldom and (as it were) only accidentally find, that these embryological categories coincide with the lines of “natural” or “phylogenetic” classification which have been arrived at by the systematic zoologist.
claims.scope: early embryonic development of animals
claims.candidate_data: Comparative datasets of egg size and cleavage type mapped onto animal phylogenies (Open Tree of Life; published egg-size compilations on Dryad).

claims.section: The cell as a sphere of action
claims.label: Surface tension gives the cell its outline and morphological individuality
claims.claim: The cell is a sphere of action of localised forces, of which surface tension gives the cell its outline and individuality; partial versus total segmentation of eggs, and unicellular versus multicellular organisation, differ in whether surface tensions succeed in forming visible separations between cells.
claims.quote: surface-tension is the particular force which is especially responsible for giving to the cell its outline and its morphological individuality.
claims.scope: cells, segmenting eggs, Infusoria and small Turbellaria
claims.candidate_data: Published measurements of cortical and interfacial tension in embryos combined with embryo imaging datasets.

claims.label: The centrosome is essentially a centre of force, not necessarily a material body
claims.claim: The centrosome is essentially a dynamic centre of force, which may or may not consist of a visible concentration of matter but tends to produce one, as shown by cells that live without visible centrosomes and centrosomes that disappear and form anew.
claims.quote: We may safely take it that the centrosome, or the “attraction sphere,” is essentially a “centre of force,” and that this dynamic centre may or may not be constituted by (but will be very apt to produce) a concrete and visible concentration of matter.
claims.scope: centrosomes of animal and plant cells
claims.candidate_data: Published studies of acentrosomal spindles and de novo centriole formation, and cell imaging datasets (Allen Cell Explorer).

claims.label: A continuous field of force shapes the whole organism regardless of its cells
claims.claim: The multicellular organism is not a colony of independent cells: a continuous field of force runs through the entire organism, not restricted to protoplasmic continuity, and shapes it independently of the number, size and form of its cells.
claims.quote: And such a continuous field of force, somehow shaping the whole organism, independently of the number, magnitude and form of the individual cells, which enter, like a froth, into its fabric, seems to me certainly and obviously to exist.
claims.scope: multicellular plants and animals
measurable_quantities: organ shape versus cell number and cell size
effect of altered cell size or number on organ form
claims.candidate_data: Published experiments on polyploid or cell-number-altered organisms (e.g. plant leaf and Drosophila wing size studies) with organ morphometrics.

claims.section: Growth by imbibition versus crystal growth
claims.label: Fluid protoplasm growing by imbibition produces rounded rather than plane surfaces
claims.claim: Because protoplasm is fluid and grows by imbibition (intussusception) rather than by deposition of particles on a surface, freely growing organisms tend to have swelling, rounded contours, and plane surfaces are rare in them unless produced by pressure.
claims.quote: So far then, as growth goes on, unaffected by pressure or other external force, the fluidity of protoplasm, its mobility internal and external, and the manner in which particles move with comparative freedom from place to place within, all manifestly tend to the production of swelling, rounded surfaces, and to their great predominance over plane surfaces in the contour of the organism.
claims.scope: living cells and organisms growing free of external pressure, contrasted with crystals
measurable_quantities: proportion of curved versus planar surface in cell and organism outlines
claims.candidate_data: 3D cell segmentation and shape datasets such as the Allen Cell Explorer and Image Data Resource, compared with crystal morphology databases.

claims.section: Surface tension and the forms of cells
claims.label: Surface tension is probably the paramount force determining cell form
claims.claim: Of the physical forces that determine the forms of cells, solitary or in contact, surface tension is of great and probably paramount importance, usually acting together with gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis.
claims.quote: Among the forces which determine the forms of cells, whether they be solitary or arranged in contact with one another, this force of surface-tension is certainly of great, and is probably of paramount importance.
claims.scope: all cells, solitary or in aggregates
claims.candidate_data: Published micropipette aspiration and AFM measurements of cortical tension paired with cell shape imaging, e.g. Allen Cell Explorer and Image Data Resource datasets.

claims.label: Organic symmetry reflects equilibrium and is absent without it, as in amoeba
claims.claim: Symmetry is highly characteristic of organic forms because they are figures of equilibrium governed by a principle of minimal energy, as in liquid films; symmetry is lacking only where equilibrium is lacking, as in the amoeba.
claims.quote: Such symmetry is in a high degree characteristic of organic forms, and is rarely absent in living things,—save in such cases as amoeba, where the equilibrium on which symmetry depends is likewise lacking.
claims.scope: organic forms generally, especially cells
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse cell shape datasets (e.g. Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) allowing comparison of symmetry measures between motile and resting cells.

claims.section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
claims.label: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility
claims.claim: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.
claims.quote: When any drop of protoplasm, either over all its surface or at some free end, as at the extremity of the pseudopodium of an amoeba, is seen likewise to “round itself off,” that is not an effect of “vital contractility,” but (as Hofmeister shewed so long ago as 1867) a simple consequence of surface tension
claims.scope: naked protoplasm, amoeboid cells and pseudopodia
measurable_quantities: effect of inhibiting active contractile machinery on rounding
claims.candidate_data: Published cell-rounding and cortical tension measurements with and without myosin inhibition; live-imaging datasets in the Image Data Resource.

claims.section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
claims.label: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena
claims.claim: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.
claims.quote: When we find that a plasmodium of Aethalium, for instance, creeps towards a damp spot, or towards a warm spot, or towards substances that happen to be nutritious, and again creeps away from solutions of sugar or of salt, we seem to be dealing with phenomena every one of which can be paralleled by ordinary phenomena of surface tension
claims.scope: slime-mould plasmodia and amoeboid organisms
measurable_quantities: direction and speed of migration in gradients
local surface tension of the plasmodium
claims.candidate_data: Published Physarum chemotaxis and thermotaxis assays and tension/rheology measurements; none known as a central database.

claims.section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
claims.label: Resting cells are spherical; the amoeboid phase is one of activity and unequal tensions
claims.claim: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.
claims.quote: In the case of the naked protoplasmic cell, as the amoeboid phase is emphatically a phase of freedom and activity, of chemical and physiological change, so, on the other hand, is the spherical form indicative of a phase of rest or comparative inactivity.
claims.scope: naked protoplasmic cells, amoebae and other protists with resting stages
claims.candidate_data: Imaging and encystment studies of Acanthamoeba and other amoebae; Image Data Resource time-lapse datasets.

claims.section: Budding yeast and localised tension changes
claims.label: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claims.claim: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.
claims.quote: When a “bud” appears, whether with or without actual growth by osmosis or otherwise of the mass, it does so because at a certain part of the cell-surface the surface tension has more or less suddenly diminished, and the area of that portion expands accordingly
claims.scope: budding yeast cells
measurable_quantities: local cell-wall or membrane tension and extensibility at the bud site
claims.candidate_data: Yeast cell-wall mechanics (AFM) and bud morphology imaging, e.g. SCMD (Saccharomyces cerevisiae Morphological Database).

claims.label: Each new foraminiferal chamber is a surface-tension figure; the whole shell is not
claims.claim: In multichambered organisms such as the foraminifera Globigerina or Rotalia, and in desmids, each newly formed bud or chamber is a figure of equilibrium shaped by surface tension while still fluid, and is then solidified onto earlier chambers, so the whole organism is not itself a figure of minimal area.
claims.quote: The little organism as a whole is not a figure of equilibrium or of minimal area; but each new bud or separate chamber is such a figure, conditioned by the forces of surface tension, and superposed upon the complex aggregate of similar bubbles after these latter have become consolidated one by one into a rigid system.
claims.scope: multichambered foraminifera, desmids and other organisms formed by successive stages of growth and consolidation
measurable_quantities: shape of individual chambers (closeness to constant-mean-curvature surfaces)
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT foraminiferal shell scans in MorphoSource and published 3D chamber reconstructions; Endless Forams image collection.

claims.label: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms
claims.claim: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.
claims.quote: in other words it will be small or minute organisms, or the small cellular elements of larger organisms, whose forms will be governed by surface-tension; while the general forms of the larger organisms will be due to other and non-molecular forces.
claims.scope: organisms and cells across sizes
measurable_quantities: agreement of shape with surface-tension figures
claims.candidate_data: Cell and organism size and shape compilations (e.g. Allen Cell Explorer for cells, AnimalTraits for body size) combined with shape measurements.

claims.section: Plateau's surfaces of revolution in cells
claims.label: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms
