claims.claim: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.
claims.notation: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const}; surfaces of revolution: plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid
claims.quote: That spheres, cylinders and unduloids are of the commonest occurrence among the forms of small unicellular organism, or of individual cells in the simpler aggregates, and that in the processes of growth, reproduction and development transitions are frequent from one of these forms to another, is obvious to the naturalist
claims.scope: unicellular organisms and cells of simple aggregates
measurable_quantities: fit of cell outlines to sphere, cylinder and unduloid profiles
claims.candidate_data: Protist and bacterial image collections (e.g. EcoTaxa plankton images, Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) analysed for shape classes.

claims.label: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claims.claim: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.
claims.notation: R_{cap} = 2R; cap subtends a cone of 60^\circ; cap height = R(2 - \sqrt{3}) \approx 0.27R
claims.quote: the normal height of the spherical cap over the end of the cylindrical cell is just a very little more than one-eighth of the diameter of the cylinder, or of the radius of the sphere. And these are the proportions which we recognise, under normal circumstances, in such a case as the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra where its free end is capped by a portion of a sphere.
claims.scope: cylindrical cells with free spherical ends, e.g. Spirogyra and other filamentous algae
claims.candidate_data: Micrographs of filamentous algae and of rod-shaped bacteria pole geometry from published imaging datasets (e.g. Image Data Resource).

claims.section: Instability of liquid cylinders and beading
claims.label: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claims.claim: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.
claims.notation: liquid cylinder of radius r unstable for length l > 2\pi r; breaks into equal, equally spaced beads
claims.quote: But this liquid cylinder has its limit of stability when its length equals its own circumference, and therefore just at the points so defined it tends to disrupt into separate segments
claims.scope: viscid capture threads of orb-weaving spiders; liquid films on fibres
claims.candidate_data: Published measurements of glue droplet spacing and size on orb-web capture threads (including datasets deposited on Dryad).

claims.label: Notched hydroid cups and annulated stems are both due to surface tension
claims.claim: The notching of the rim of hydroid calycles and the annular constrictions of their cylindrical stems are phenomena of the same order, both produced by surface tension acting on the structures while they are still fluid or semifluid films, as in the beaded rim of a splash.
claims.quote: In the case of the hydroid calycle (Fig. 72), we are led to the conclusion that the two common and conspicuous features of notching or indentation of the cup, and of constriction or annulation of the long cylindrical stem, are phenomena of the same order and are due to surface-tension in both cases alike.
claims.scope: calycles and stems of campanularian hydroids and other small organic cups
measurable_quantities: number and spacing of rim teeth relative to rim circumference
annulation spacing relative to stem diameter
claims.candidate_data: Hydroid specimen images in museum collections and GBIF-linked media, with morphometric measurement.

claims.label: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claims.claim: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.
claims.quote: I take it therefore, that the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra, or any other cylindrical cell which grows in freedom from any manifest external restraint, has assumed that particular form simply by reason of the molecular constitution of its developing surface-membrane; and that this molecular constitution was anisotropous, in such a way as to render extension easier in one direction than another.
claims.scope: elongated plant cells, algae, yeasts and other walled cells grown free of external restraint
claims.candidate_data: Published cellulose microfibril orientation and wall mechanics data for algal and plant cells; Plant Cell Atlas imaging resources.

claims.section: Limited range of forms in small organisms
claims.label: Small organisms show a limited range of forms because molecular forces control them
claims.claim: Because protozoa, bacteria and other minute cells are of a size at which form is mainly controlled by molecular forces, they exhibit only a limited range of forms, which vary with physical conditions.
claims.quote: To the fact that these little organisms belong to an order of magnitude in which form is mainly, if not wholly, conditioned and controlled by molecular forces, is due the limited range of forms which they actually exhibit.
claims.scope: unicellular organisms, bacteria, spores and free cells
measurable_quantities: morphological disparity (shape diversity) versus organism size
claims.candidate_data: Large plankton and microbial image sets (e.g. EcoTaxa) and bacterial shape compilations compared with metazoan morphospace data from Phenoscape or MorphoSource.

claims.section: Limited range of forms in small organisms
claims.label: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claims.claim: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.
claims.quote: Whatever grounds we may have for attributing to these organisms a permanent or stable specific identity (after the fashion of the higher plants and animals), we can seldom safely do so on the ground of definite and always recognisable _form_
claims.scope: bacteria and micrococci
claims.candidate_data: Bacterial cell morphology imaging datasets across growth conditions (e.g. published Dryad and Image Data Resource collections) paired with species identity.

claims.label: Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids
claims.claim: The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.
claims.notation: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const} (unduloid between two unequal supporting rings)
claims.quote: The cups of the various species of Vorticella (Fig. 75) are nothing in the world but a beautiful series of unduloids, or partial unduloids, in every gradation from a form that is all but cylindrical to one that is all but a perfect sphere.
claims.scope: Vorticella and other cup-shaped or flask-shaped ciliates and flagellates
measurable_quantities: ratio of neck to bulge radius
claims.candidate_data: Ciliate micrograph collections (e.g. EcoTaxa, published Vorticella morphometric studies) for outline fitting.

claims.label: Protozoan loricas form by adsorption into least-area surfaces, not for protection
claims.claim: The membranous cups (loricas) of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa arise inevitably from substances adsorbed in the surface layer of the protoplasm, and molecular forces make the resulting pellicle a surface of least possible area under the circumstances, here an unduloid; this efficient cause, rather than a protective purpose, explains their form.
claims.quote: that this surface pellicle or membrane was inevitably bound, by molecular forces, to become a surface of the least possible area which the circumstances permitted
claims.scope: loricate protozoa such as Salpingoeca, Tintinnus, Dinobryon and Codonella
claims.candidate_data: Tintinnid lorica morphometric datasets and plankton imaging collections such as EcoTaxa.

claims.label: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent
claims.claim: The assumption that similar or identical forms indicate genealogical relationship is far less well founded for minute organisms with few, simple characters whose form is largely produced directly by a physical force, so identical forms of such organisms in different times or places need not indicate unbroken descent or common stock.
claims.quote: when we attempt to extend it to minute organisms whose specific characters are few and simple, whose simplicity becomes much more manifest when we regard it from the point of view of physical and mathematical description and analysis, and whose form is referable, or (to say the least of it) is very largely referable, to the direct and immediate action of a particular physical force.
claims.scope: minute organisms such as foraminifera (e.g. Lagena), infusoria and radiolaria
claims.candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of foraminifera and ciliates (e.g. PR2 ribosomal database, GenBank sequences) compared with morphospecies assignments and fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database.

claims.section: Foraminiferal shells and position of symmetry
claims.label: The unduloid Lagena shell is formed while hanging vertically in the sea
claims.claim: The flask-shaped (unduloid) shell of Lagena is formed while the organism hangs vertically, in a position of symmetry about its vertical axis, like a hanging drop; flattened or winged forms are those formed when this symmetry of position was absent and the shell lay horizontally.
claims.quote: but we may be pretty sure that it is suspended vertically in the sea, that is to say in a position of symmetry as regards its vertical axis, about which the unduloid surface of revolution is symmetrically formed.
claims.scope: monothalamous calcareous foraminifera (Lagena) and, by extension, flask-shaped pteropod shells
measurable_quantities: orientation of living organism during shell formation
presence of lateral flattening or wings
claims.candidate_data: Field and culture observations of Lagena life position and shell morphometrics from foraminiferal collections; none known as a database.

claims.label: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely
claims.claim: Small tension changes in a thin-walled elongated cell produce wrinkling in the plane of greatest curvature, hence longitudinal fluting, especially near the ends; where the wall is thick relative to diameter, as in the narrow neck of Lagena or tubular hydroid gonangia, bending stiffness makes folding transverse instead.
claims.quote: The manner in which our little Lagena-shell tends to fold or wrinkle, longitudinally in its wider part, and transversely or annularly in its narrow neck, is thus completely and easily explained.
claims.scope: Lagena and other foraminifera, campanularian gonangia, and similar thin-walled elongated organic vesicles
claims.candidate_data: Foraminiferal shell images and micro-CT in MorphoSource and museum collections, measured for fold orientation and wall thickness.

claims.label: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially
claims.claim: Fluid surface protoplasm creeps up the stiff axial filaments of a heliozoan such as Actinophrys, and because this surface-tension pull is symmetrical around each filament the filaments are set normal to the cell surface, radiating from the centre; closely spaced filaments produce honeycomb-like depressions between them.
claims.quote: Since the attraction exercised by this surface tension is symmetrical around the filament, the latter will be pulled equally in all directions; in other words it will tend to be set normally to the surface of the sphere, that is to say radiating directly outwards from the centre.
claims.scope: Heliozoa and radiolarians with radiating axopodia or spicules
measurable_quantities: angle of axopodia to cell surface
contact-angle profile of protoplasm on filaments
claims.candidate_data: Published imaging of heliozoan axopodia; no dedicated database known.

claims.label: The trypanosome undulating membrane is a liquid film drawn up along a flagellum
claims.claim: The undulating membrane of trypanosomes and related flagellates forms when the flagellum lies near and parallel to the body and the fluid surface protoplasm is drawn up as a film along it, as a soap-film would be; the membrane is thus a liquid film of constant mean curvature whose undulations are produced by molecular tensions, not by its own active mobility.
claims.notation: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const} (undulating membrane as a liquid film)
claims.quote: It is a plausible assumption to suppose that, as the flagellum waves about, it comes to lie near and parallel to the body of the cell, and that the frill or undulating membrane is formed by the clear, fluid protoplasm of the surface layer springing up in a film to run up and along the flagellum, just as a soap-film would be formed in similar circumstances.
claims.scope: trypanosomes, Trichomonas and related flagellates, and spermatozoa with undulating membranes
claims.candidate_data: Electron microscopy and live imaging of trypanosome and Trichomonas morphology, e.g. the TrypTag localisation resource and the Image Data Resource.

claims.label: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure
claims.claim: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sphere in diluted blood.
claims.notation: biconcave corpuscle: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 \neq \text{const}, so not a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone
claims.quote: Accordingly, from the point of view of surface tension alone, the blood-corpuscle is not a surface of equilibrium; or in other words, it is not a fluid drop suspended in another liquid.
claims.scope: mammalian and other vertebrate red blood cells
claims.candidate_data: Published erythrocyte shape and osmotic fragility datasets and red cell membrane mechanics measurements.

claims.label: Decapod sperm-cell shape is an intermediate phase of osmotic shrinkage
claims.claim: The normal form of decapod crustacean sperm-cells is one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage from a spherical form, caused by osmotic withdrawal of fluid without a matching reduction of surface area, so that equivalent shapes are produced by salt solutions of equivalent (molecular-weight-proportional) concentration.
claims.quote: we see that what we call its normal appearance is just one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage, brought about by the abstraction of fluid from its interior as the result of an osmotic pressure greater outside than inside the cell
claims.scope: sperm-cells of decapod crustacea (Inachus, Galathea, Dromia, crayfish) and, by comparison, red blood cells
measurable_quantities: cell shape as a function of external osmolarity
claims.candidate_data: Published osmotic-response studies of decapod spermatozoa; no dedicated database known.

claims.label: Elastic fibrillae act as a microscopic skeleton shaping spiral cells
claims.claim: The spiral and other peculiar forms of decapod sperm-cells and of many Infusoria are produced by more or less elastic fibrillae in the cell, which restrain and modify the surface forces like the wire frames and coils in Plateau's experiments, acting as a microscopic skeleton.
claims.quote: In all probability we must in like manner attribute the peculiar spiral and other forms, for instance of many Infusoria, to the presence, among the multitudinous other differentiations of their protoplasmic substance, of such more or less elastic fibrillae, which play as it were the part of a microscopic skeleton
claims.scope: Infusoria, decapod sperm-cells and other cells with non-equilibrium shapes
measurable_quantities: presence and arrangement of cortical fibrillar structures
change of shape when fibrils are disrupted
claims.candidate_data: Electron microscopy and cytoskeleton imaging of ciliates and sperm cells, e.g. the Cell Image Library and EMPIAR.

claims.label: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface
claims.claim: The so-called secretion of a cell-wall or membrane is the adsorption of certain constituents of the cell, which lower surface tension, to its surface (as formulated by the Gibbs-Thomson law), where they also increase viscosity and rigidity; the formation of a cell membrane is thus a chemico-physical phenomenon.
claims.quote: The so-called “secretion” of this cell-wall is nothing more than a sort of exudation, or striving towards the surface, of certain constituent molecules or particles within the cell; and the Gibbs-Thomson law formulates, in part at least, the conditions under which they do so.
claims.scope: cell-walls and membranes of protozoa, plant cells and blood corpuscles
measurable_quantities: surface concentration of wall materials during wall formation
claims.candidate_data: Biochemical and imaging studies of cell-wall deposition; no single database known.

claims.label: Spicules are deposited at interfaces between cells or vacuoles
claims.claim: Skeletal spicules, as in sponges and radiolaria, are characteristically deposited in the interfacial boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and their form is in many cases regulated by the arrangement of these boundaries.
claims.quote: it is highly characteristic of the whole process of spicule-formation for the deposits to be laid down just in the “interfacial” boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and that the form of the spicular structures tends in many cases to be regulated and determined by the arrangement of these boundaries.
claims.scope: spicule-forming organisms, especially sponges and radiolaria
measurable_quantities: location of spicule deposition relative to cell and vacuole boundaries
correspondence of spicule geometry with boundary geometry
claims.candidate_data: Electron microscopy of sponge sclerocytes and radiolarian skeletogenesis (e.g. EMPIAR, Cell Image Library) and radiolarian image collections.

claims.label: Membranes and cysts form only after protoplasm rounds up with positive surface tension
claims.claim: Because adsorption requires a surface tension greater than zero, films or threads of creeping protoplasm do not form an encysting membrane, and an organism forms its cyst or cell-wall only when its protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension and gathered into a roughly spherical body.
claims.quote: It is for this reason that films or threads of creeping protoplasm shew little tendency, or none, to cover themselves with an encysting membrane; and that it is only when, in an altered phase, the protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension, and has accordingly gathered itself up into a more or less spherical body, that the tendency to form a membrane is manifested
claims.scope: amoeboid and plasmodial protists that encyst
measurable_quantities: timing of cyst-wall deposition relative to cell rounding
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse encystment studies of Acanthamoeba, Entamoeba or Physarum; Image Data Resource time-lapse datasets.

claims.label: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption
claims.claim: Since a rise of temperature reduces adsorbability (and surface tension), lower temperature favours adsorption and membrane formation, which probably accounts for the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter and the strong shells or capsules of winter eggs.
claims.quote: We may in all probability ascribe to this fact and to its converse, or at least associate with it, such phenomena as the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter, or the frequent formation of strong shells or membranous capsules in “winter-eggs.”
claims.scope: encysting protists and invertebrates producing winter or resting eggs
measurable_quantities: egg shell thickness versus temperature or season
claims.candidate_data: Published Daphnia ephippia and rotifer resting-egg induction experiments and protist encystment-temperature studies (e.g. Dryad datasets).

claims.label: Chondriosomes and similar fibrils are surface-tension clumps drawn along the cell axis
claims.claim: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force and dynamical polarity in the cell.
claims.quote: while, from the physical point of view we are tempted to see but little mystery in the whole phenomenon, and to ascribe it, in all probability and in general terms, to the gathering or “clumping” together, under surface tension, of various constituents of the heterogeneous cell-content, and to the drawing out of these little clumps along the axis of the cell towards one or other of its extremities
claims.scope: fibrillar and granular cytoplasmic structures of epithelial, gland, nerve and germ cells
measurable_quantities: orientation of mitochondria relative to cell axis
dependence of their arrangement on cytoplasmic flows
claims.candidate_data: Mitochondrial imaging in the Allen Cell Explorer and Human Protein Atlas subcellular atlas, with studies of cytoplasmic streaming.

claims.label: Potassium salts concentrate where cell-surface tension is weak
claims.claim: Potassium salts, like inorganic substances generally, raise surface tension and therefore concentrate at those parts of a cell surface where the tension is weak, so their localised accumulation (shown by Macallum's cobalt-nitrite method) indicates inequalities of surface tension.
claims.quote: and we may safely take it that our potassium salts, like inorganic substances in general, tend to _raise_ the surface tension, and will therefore be found concentrating at a portion of the surface whose tension is weak
claims.scope: plant and animal cells, solitary and in tissues
measurable_quantities: local potassium concentration at cell surfaces
claims.candidate_data: Potassium-sensitive fluorescent indicator imaging and X-ray microanalysis studies of cells; no dedicated database known.

claims.label: Conjugation outgrowths and root-hairs arise at sites of potassium concentration
claims.claim: The bulges that begin conjugation in algae such as Pleurocarpus and Mesocarpus, and the root-hair outgrowth of Equisetum spores, arise where surface tension is weakened, and these sites coincide with heavy concentrations of potassium salts, which disperse when the cell becomes symmetrical again.
claims.quote: This bulge is, in the first place, a sign of weakened surface tension on one side of the cell, which as a whole had hitherto been a symmetrical cylinder; in the second place, we see that the bulging area corresponds to the position of a great concentration of the potassic salt
claims.scope: conjugating zygnematacean algae, germinating Equisetum spores and other cells forming local outgrowths
measurable_quantities: potassium concentration at outgrowth sites versus elsewhere
timing of potassium accumulation relative to bulging
claims.candidate_data: Ion imaging studies of tip growth in root hairs and pollen tubes and of algal conjugation; no dedicated database known.

claims.label: Potassium accumulates at the bases of cilia and flagella
claims.claim: Ciliate and flagellate cells show a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of their cilia, which accounts (through weakened surface tension) for the small protuberance where a flagellum arises and the ridge at the base of a row of cilia.
claims.quote: In the case of ciliate or flagellate cells, there is to be found a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of the cilia.
claims.scope: ciliated and flagellated cells, e.g. Vorticella and monads
measurable_quantities: local surface protrusion at flagellar base
claims.candidate_data: Ion imaging and elemental microanalysis of ciliated cells; ciliary proteomics resources such as CiliaCarta do not directly address ions.

claims.label: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces
claims.claim: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.
claims.quote: we have arrived at the conclusion, as regards unicellular organisms, that not only their general configuration but also _their departures from symmetry_ may be correlated with the molecular forces manifested in their fluid or semi-fluid surfaces.
claims.scope: unicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: spatial distribution of surface tension or cortical tension
claims.candidate_data: Combined cell-shape imaging (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) and cortical tension mapping studies.

claims.label: Forms of cell-aggregates are shaped chiefly by surface tension toward minimal areas
claims.claim: The forms of cells in contact with one another, and ultimately of tissues, are determined especially by surface tension, which shows itself in the production of surfaces of (relatively) minimal area.
claims.quote: we shall probably find, and we may at least begin by assuming, that the agency of surface tension is especially manifest and important. The effect of this surface tension will chiefly manifest itself in the production of surfaces _minimae areae_
claims.scope: cell-aggregates and tissues of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: total interface area relative to minimal configurations
claims.candidate_data: Segmented 2D and 3D tissue images (e.g. Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer) combined with published cortical-tension and laser-ablation measurements of cell interfaces.

claims.section: Three surfaces in contact and Sachs’s Rule
claims.label: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form
claims.claim: Plant cell walls often meet at right angles (Sachs’s Rule) because an earlier wall has usually become solid and rigid before a later partition joins it, so the fluid partition sets itself at equal angles, i.e. perpendicular, to the rigid wall.
claims.notation: fluid partition meets a rigid wall at 90^\circ (Sachs's rule)
claims.quote: such validity as the rule possesses is due to the fact that among plant-tissues it very frequently happens that one cell-wall has become solid and rigid before another and later partition-wall is developed in connection with it.
claims.scope: plant tissues with rigid cell walls
measurable_quantities: angle at which new partitions meet existing walls
rigidity of parent wall at time of division
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse confocal imaging of plant meristems and segmented plant tissue datasets (e.g. published Arabidopsis shoot-apex segmentations on public repositories) giving junction angles of new versus old walls.

claims.label: Shape of paired cells depends on relative tensions at outer surface and partition
claims.claim: Whether two adjacent cells in a filament (as in Nostoc and its allies) are separated by flat partitions, are hemispherical, or are each more than a hemisphere depends on the relative magnitudes of the tension at the outer cell surface and at the boundary between the cells.
claims.quote: These various conditions depend, according to what we have already learned, upon the relative magnitudes of the tensions at the surface of the cells and at the boundary between them
claims.scope: pairs and chains of cells in filamentous lower algae and other two-celled aggregates
measurable_quantities: partition diameter relative to cell diameter
ratio of cell–cell to cell–medium surface tension
claims.candidate_data: Published micropipette and contact-angle measurements of cell doublets, and microscopy images of cyanobacterial filaments from public image collections.

claims.label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claims.claim: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.
claims.notation: walls meet three at a time at 120^\circ, independent of cell size; relative sizes set only wall curvature
claims.quote: in both cases we see the cell-walls everywhere meeting, by threes, at angles of 120°, irrespective of the size of the individual cells: whose relative size, on the other hand, determines the _curvature_ of the partition-walls.
claims.scope: plant parenchyma, honeycomb, segmenting eggs and other cellular complexes viewed perpendicular to the walls
measurable_quantities: number of walls meeting at each vertex
wall curvature versus size difference of neighbouring cells
claims.candidate_data: Segmented epithelial and plant tissue images (e.g. Image Data Resource, published Drosophila wing-disc and plant meristem segmentations) from which vertex degree and junction angles can be measured.

claims.label: Four cells of a segmenting egg never meet in a point; a polar furrow is always present
claims.claim: In the four-celled stage of a segmenting egg whose cells are in full fluid contact, the four cells cannot meet in a single point; a short intermediate partition (the polar furrow) must be present, and reports of four cells meeting in a simple cross are due to error or imperfect observation.
claims.quote: it is quite certain that no simple and homogeneous system of fluid films such as we are dealing with is in equilibrium without its presence.
claims.scope: four-celled stage of segmenting eggs of animals in which blastomeres are in full fluid contact
measurable_quantities: presence and length of polar (cross) furrow
number of cells meeting at the animal and vegetal poles
claims.candidate_data: Live-imaging and 3D segmentation datasets of early cleavage-stage embryos (e.g. published ascidian, sea urchin and frog embryo atlases) in which pole junction topology can be scored.

claims.section: Unequal tensions and rounding of blastomeres
claims.label: Strong cell–cell tension relative to cell–medium tension makes cells round off
claims.claim: Where the tension at cell–cell contacts exceeds that at cell–medium surfaces, the external angle between neighbouring cells is less than 120°, and if the cell–cell tension equals or exceeds the sum of the other two the cells touch only at a point, which explains rounded-off blastomeres separated by spaces.
claims.notation: T_{cc} > T_{cm} \Rightarrow external angle < 120^\circ; T_{cc} \ge T_{cm} + T'_{cm} \Rightarrow contact only at a point
claims.quote: If the former be greater than either of the other two, the outside angle will be less than 120°; and if the tension along the surface _cc′_ be as much or more than the sum of the other two, then the drops will stand in contact only, save for the possible effect of external pressure, at a point.
claims.scope: blastomeres of segmenting eggs, pollen tetrads and filamentous algae in contact with a surrounding fluid
claims.candidate_data: Published measurements of blastomere contact angles and cortical tension (micropipette aspiration) in early embryos, e.g. mouse and ascidian compaction studies.

claims.section: Epidermal layer as a positional effect
claims.label: An epidermis’s physical characters follow simply from its lying on the outside
claims.claim: The fundamental character of an epidermis is that it lies on the outside of the cell mass, and its main physical features (flattened, rectangular cells meeting partitions at near right angles) follow from that position through unequal and consolidated tensions in its outer walls.
claims.quote: the fundamental character of an epidermis simply is that it lies on the outside, and that its main physical characteristics follow, as a matter of course, from the position which it occupies and from the various consequences which that situation entails.
claims.scope: epidermal tissue of plants (especially simple epidermal tissue as in Laminaria) and analogous outer cell layers
measurable_quantities: shape and aspect ratio of outer versus inner cells
angles at which anticlinal walls meet the outer wall
claims.candidate_data: Segmented plant tissue sections and confocal stacks in public image repositories (e.g. Image Data Resource) comparing outer-layer and inner-layer cell geometry.

claims.label: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
claims.claim: Perfectly regular hexagonal cell patterns occur only where the cells are uniform in size and subject to uniform forces, as in the retinal pigment epithelium; where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma) or growth adds directional traction, the hexagons become irregular or elongated.
claims.quote: the cells, uniform in size, are flattened out to a uniform thickness by the fluid pressure acting radially; and their reaction on each other converts the flattened discs into regular hexagons.
claims.scope: animal epithelia (retinal pigment epithelium, intestinal and vascular epithelium) and plant epidermis
measurable_quantities: coefficient of variation of cell area
claims.candidate_data: Published retinal pigment epithelium flat-mount morphometry datasets and segmented intestinal epithelium images in public repositories such as Image Data Resource.

claims.label: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons
claims.claim: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.
claims.notation: uniform pressure on similar cylinders or spheres \Rightarrow hexagons, 6 neighbours, angles 120^\circ
claims.quote: wherever we have a system of cylinders or spheres, associated together with sufficient mutual interaction to bring them into complete surface contact, there, in section or in surface view, we tend to get a pattern of hexagons.
claims.scope: epithelia, plant parenchyma, coral corallites, insect combs and other close-packed bodies of uniform size
claims.candidate_data: Segmented epithelial images (e.g. Image Data Resource) giving polygon-number distributions, and coral specimen images in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Close-packed corallites of varying size are on average hexagonal
claims.claim: In colonial corals whose corallites are in close contact, the corallites are squeezed into hexagonal prisms; where their sizes vary irregularly they are hexagonal on average, some having fewer and some more than six sides, while loosely bundled corallites stay cylindrical.
claims.quote: where there is greater and more irregular variation in size, the cells will be _on the average_ hexagonal, but some will have fewer and some more sides than six
claims.scope: massive versus fasciculate colonial corals (e.g. Lithostrotion, Cyathophyllum, Arachnophyllum)
claims.candidate_data: Coral specimen images and 3D scans in MorphoSource and fossil occurrence and growth-form data in the Paleobiology Database.

claims.label: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets
claims.claim: The hive-bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism closed at one end by three rhombic facets of a rhombic dodecahedron meeting at about 109° 28′, the configuration that encloses a given volume with the least surface.
claims.notation: hexagonal prism closed by three rhombic facets at 109^\circ 28' (\cos\theta = -1/3); minimal surface for given volume
claims.quote: The bee’s cell, then, is this figure incompletely formed: it is a hexagonal prism with one open or unfinished end, and one trihedral apex of a rhombic dodecahedron.
claims.scope: comb cells of the hive-bee
measurable_quantities: rhomb angles at the base of the cell
wax surface area per unit cell volume
claims.candidate_data: Published micro-CT studies of honeybee comb geometry and 3D scans of combs; no single standard repository known.

claims.label: Comb geometry arises from surface tension in semi-fluid wax, not bee design
claims.claim: The regular hexagonal and pyramidal geometry of the bee’s comb is produced automatically by surface tension acting on the cell walls while the wax (or the wasp’s paper pulp) is still semi-fluid, the insects merely building thin tubular cells packed closely together; it is not due to the bee seeking to economise wax.
claims.quote: It seems more likely that we have to do with a true surface-tension effect; in other words, that the walls assume their configuration when in a semi-fluid state, while the papery pulp is still liquid, or while the wax is warm under the high temperature of the crowded hive
claims.scope: comb-building social bees and wasps
measurable_quantities: cell shape at initial construction versus later
claims.candidate_data: Published thermography and time-lapse studies of honeybee comb construction; no dedicated public database known.

claims.label: Parenchyma cells are generally rhombic dodecahedra, ideal froths tetrakaidecahedra
claims.claim: A perfectly fluid froth of equal cells is divided into Kelvin’s fourteen-sided tetrakaidecahedra, but in plant parenchyma, given restraint and imperfect fluidity, the cells generally take the rhombic dodecahedral form even under symmetrical conditions.
claims.quote: Accordingly, it is very probably the case that, in the parenchymatous tissue, under the actual conditions of restraint and of very imperfect fluidity, it is after all the rhombic dodecahedral configuration which, even under perfectly symmetrical conditions, is generally assumed.
claims.scope: isolated cells of symmetrical plant parenchyma of near-equal cell size
measurable_quantities: number of quadrilateral, pentagonal and hexagonal faces
claims.candidate_data: 3D segmented plant tissue volumes from confocal or micro-CT imaging in public repositories (e.g. Image Data Resource), giving face counts per cell.

claims.label: Physical laws govern the whole configuration of later-stage segmenting eggs
claims.claim: The whole configuration of an egg in advanced stages of segmentation is determined by simple physical laws just as in the two- and four-celled stages, even though the mathematics becomes too difficult to follow.
claims.quote: We have little reason to doubt, and no just cause to disbelieve, that the whole configuration, for instance of an egg in the advanced stages of segmentation, is accurately determined by simple physical laws
claims.scope: segmenting eggs of animals at all cleavage stages
measurable_quantities: cell positions and shapes in embryos
agreement of physical foam or vertex models with observed embryo geometry
claims.candidate_data: Published 3D cell-shape atlases of early embryos (e.g. C. elegans and ascidian embryo segmentations) compared against foam and vertex-model simulations.

claims.section: Polar furrow variants and cell size
claims.label: Polar-furrow arrangements follow relative cell sizes, not species identity
claims.claim: Small changes in the relative sizes of the four cells carry the median partition and its polar furrows through all their possible arrangements, which correspond to those observed in various embryos; these arrangements are physical phenomena distributed without relation to zoological classification, not species characters.
claims.quote: So, by slight and delicate modifications in the relative size of the cells, we may pass through all the possible arrangements of the median partition, and of the “furrows” which correspond to its upper and lower edges; and every one of these arrangements has been frequently observed in the four-celled stage of various embryos.
claims.scope: four-celled stage of embryos across molluscs, annelids, coelenterates, vertebrates and others
measurable_quantities: upper and lower polar furrow lengths
claims.candidate_data: Published blastomere volume and cleavage-geometry measurements from imaging studies of early spiralian, ascidian and frog embryos.

claims.label: No evidence that physical forces give way to unknown vital agencies in development
claims.claim: Although forces other than surface tension act in a growing embryo, there is no evidence at any stage that physical forces cease to govern its material form and are replaced by agencies unknown to physics.
claims.quote: But we have no evidence whatsoever that at this point, or that point, or at any, the dominion of the physical forces over the material system gives place to a new condition where agencies at present unknown to the physicist impose themselves on the living matter
claims.scope: developing embryos and living tissues generally
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles
claims.claim: For a rectangular cell to be divided equally by a partition of least area, the partition must cut across its longest axis, and in successive bisections each new partition must be at right angles to the one before.
claims.notation: minimal bisecting partition of a rectangular cell \perp longest axis; successive partitions mutually \perp
claims.quote: From this we may draw the simple rule that, for a rectangular body or parallelopiped to be divided equally by means of a partition of minimal area, (1) the partition must cut across the longest axis of the figure; and (2) in the event of successive bisections, each partition must run at right angles to its immediate predecessor.
claims.scope: dividing cells of roughly rectangular shape, especially in plant tissues
measurable_quantities: orientation of division plane relative to cell long axis
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse lineage-tracked plant meristem and early embryo datasets (e.g. published Arabidopsis embryo and shoot-apex segmentations) recording division-plane orientation.

claims.section: Sachs’s and Errera’s rules of division
claims.label: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)
claims.claim: The fundamental rule of cell division is that the incipient partition of a dividing cell takes the least possible area that can divide the given volume; Sachs’s rule of successive divisions at right angles is a subordinate case of this principle.
claims.notation: partition \Sigma = \arg\min |\Sigma| subject to dividing V in the given ratio
claims.quote: a much more important and fundamental rule, due not to Sachs but to Errera; that (3) the incipient partition-wall of a dividing cell tends to be such that its area is the least possible by which the given space-content can be enclosed.
claims.scope: dividing cells, especially plant cells and blastomeres
measurable_quantities: area of alternative partitions dividing the same volume
claims.candidate_data: Published 3D segmented plant embryo and meristem datasets in which observed division planes have been compared to computed minimal-area planes.

claims.section: Unequal division of a cubical cell
claims.label: A cell cutting off under ~3/10 of its volume uses a curved corner wall, not a plane
claims.claim: When a cubical or rectangular cell divides unequally and the smaller part is less than about three-tenths of the whole, the minimal partition is a quarter-cylinder cutting off one corner rather than a plane wall; below about 0.15 of the volume a spherical octant in a corner is smaller still.
claims.notation: unequal division of a cube: quarter-cylinder in a corner minimal for V_{small}/V \lesssim 0.3; spherical octant for V_{small}/V \lesssim 0.15
claims.quote: that one portion by anything less than about three-tenths of the whole, or three-sevenths of the other portion, there will be a tendency for the cell to divide, not by means of a plane transverse partition, but by means of a curved, cylindrical wall cutting off one corner of the original cell
claims.scope: unequally dividing rectangular plant cells, e.g. hairs in Fucus conceptacles, moss paraphyses, stomatal precursor cells
claims.candidate_data: Imaging datasets of asymmetric divisions in plant epidermis (e.g. published stomatal lineage time-lapse studies) giving daughter volume ratios and wall shapes.

claims.section: Division of a flattened quadrant cell
claims.label: A quadrant-shaped flat cell divides by a curved anticlinal wall about 3:7 along its side
claims.claim: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.
claims.notation: bisecting a quadrant: circular arc \perp side and periphery, cutting off 55^\circ 22' of the arc, starting \approx 0.3r from the centre
claims.quote: Now we find that a flattened cell which is approximately a quadrant of a circle invariably divides after the manner of Fig. 145, C, that is to say, by an approximately circular, _anticlinal_ wall
claims.scope: flattened discoid algae (e.g. Erythrotrichia) and eggs flattened under pressure (frog, sea-urchin) at the eight-cell stage
measurable_quantities: position of new wall on the radial side
claims.candidate_data: Imaging of compressed early embryos and discoid algal thalli in published developmental studies; no dedicated database known.

claims.label: Sector cells divide anticlinally only between 62½° and 90°, otherwise periclinally
claims.claim: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.
claims.notation: sector cell divides anticlinally iff 62\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ \lesssim \theta \le 90^\circ, otherwise periclinally
claims.quote: We see from this, then, that what we have called an anticlinal partition, as _MP_, is only likely to occur in a triangular or prismatic cell whose angle of arc lies between 90° and 62½°. In all narrower or more tapering cells, the periclinal partition will be of less area, and will therefore be more and more likely to occur.
claims.scope: wedge-shaped cells in flattened discs, growing points and embryos of plants and flattened eggs
measurable_quantities: sector angle of the mother cell
orientation of the new partition (anticlinal or periclinal)
claims.candidate_data: Lineage-tracked plant embryo and meristem segmentations (published Arabidopsis embryo atlases) in which mother-cell geometry and division orientation can be scored.

claims.section: Uniform growth and unequal cell division
claims.label: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times
claims.claim: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).
claims.notation: after bisecting a quadrant: triangular cell reaches division size at 1.345r, quadrilateral at 1.517r
claims.quote: For it shews us that a uniform and symmetrical growth of the organism (symmetrical, that is to say, under the limitations of a plane surface, or plane section) by no means involves a uniform or symmetrical growth of the individual cells, but may, under certain conditions, actually lead to inequality among these
claims.scope: flattened discoid cell aggregates growing uniformly, such as Erythrotrichia
measurable_quantities: timing of division of sister cells
cell area growth rate by position
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse imaging of discoid algal or plant tissue growth with lineage tracking; no dedicated public dataset known.

claims.section: Origin of an epidermis by minimal-area division
claims.label: Successive minimal-area divisions leave quadrilateral cells forming an epidermis
claims.claim: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.
claims.quote: we shall consequently have a superficial or peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells, with sides approximately parallel, that is to say what we are accustomed to call _an epidermis_.
claims.scope: discoid and rounded embryonic structures of plants (moss embryos, algal discs, antheridia)
measurable_quantities: shape of peripheral versus interior cells
orientation of divisions in the outer layer
claims.candidate_data: Published segmented plant embryo atlases (e.g. Arabidopsis early embryo 3D segmentations) giving protoderm formation and division orientations.

claims.label: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species
claims.claim: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.
claims.quote: is a particular arrangement of cell-partitions to be looked upon (as the published figures of the embryologist are apt to suggest) as a _specific character_, or at least a constant or normal character, of the particular organism? The answer to this question is a direct negative
claims.scope: eight-celled stage of eggs, especially the animal pole of the frog’s egg
measurable_quantities: frequency of each eight-cell arrangement type within a species
claims.candidate_data: Large samples of imaged Xenopus or other amphibian eight-cell embryos from published developmental imaging studies; Xenbase may hold relevant images.

claims.label: All surface groupings of eight cells belong to one of thirteen types
claims.claim: Because n cells sharing a common outer boundary and meeting three at a time need n − 3 intermediate partitions, every possible grouping of eight cells all reaching the surface belongs to one of thirteen topological types, so all drawings of such eight-celled structures represent one of these types.
claims.notation: n cells meeting three at a time with a common outer boundary need n - 3 partitions; n = 8 gives 13 types
claims.quote: all possible groupings or arrangements whatsoever of eight cells (where all take part in the _surface_ of the group, none being submerged or wholly enveloped by the rest) are referable to some one or other of _thirteen_ types or forms.
claims.scope: eight-celled aggregates of plants and animals with all cells at the surface (segmenting eggs, apical cones, discs)
claims.candidate_data: Segmented images of eight-cell embryos and plant tissues from published embryo atlases, scored for junction topology.

claims.label: Most stable cell groupings spread contacts evenly; unstable ones concentrate them
claims.claim: Among the possible arrangements of a small group of cells, the most stable (and therefore commonest) are those in which the cell-to-cell contacts are most evenly divided among the cells, and the least stable are those in which one cell has a predominant number of contacts.
claims.quote: But it would appear that the most stable arrangements are those in which the total number of contacts is most evenly divided, and the least stable are those in which some one cell has, as in type _f_, a predominant number of contacts.
claims.scope: small aggregates of cells or drops (segmenting eggs, oil-drop models)
claims.candidate_data: Live-imaging datasets of early cleavage embryos and foam or emulsion experiments recording neighbour topology over time.

claims.label: Few partition patterns recur across organisms regardless of classification
claims.claim: Because a closed surface divided into a small number of faces admits only a small number of arrangements, the same few configurations of cells (and of parts and organs) recur in all kinds of plants and animals with no relation to biological classification.
claims.quote: This is the simple reason why we meet in such a case as we have been discussing (viz. the arrangement of a group or system of eight cells) with the same few types recurring again and again in all sorts of organisms, plants as well as animals, and with no relation to the lines of biological classification
claims.scope: small cell groups and partitioned organs across plants and animals
measurable_quantities: frequency of each partition topology by taxon
claims.candidate_data: Cleavage-pattern descriptions compiled across taxa from published embryological imaging, combined with phylogenies (e.g. Open Tree of Life) to test phylogenetic signal.

claims.label: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation
claims.claim: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.
claims.quote: Where a single fossula occurs, we are usually told that it is a symptom of “bilaterality”; and this is in turn interpreted as an indication of a higher grade of organisation than is implied in the purely “radial symmetry” of the commoner types of coral. The mathematical aspect of the case gives no warrant for this interpretation.
claims.scope: rugose and other corals with septa meeting one another (Heterophyllia, Zaphrentis and allies)
claims.candidate_data: Fossil coral specimen images in MorphoSource and occurrence and taxonomy data in the Paleobiology Database.

claims.label: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones
claims.claim: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).
claims.quote: It is obvious that in the case of the oblong cells of the epidermis in the hyacinth the stomata will be found arranged in regular rows, while they will be irregularly distributed over the surface of the leaf in such a case as we have depicted in Sedum.
claims.scope: leaf epidermis of monocotyledons with oblong cells and dicotyledons with polygonal cells
measurable_quantities: spatial arrangement of stomata (row alignment index)
claims.candidate_data: Leaf epidermis micrograph collections and stomatal trait datasets (e.g. TRY plant traits for stomatal density, published leaf-epidermis image datasets).

claims.label: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates
claims.claim: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.
claims.quote: the pollen-grains afterwards fall apart, and their individual form will depend upon whether or no their walls have solidified before this liberation takes place.
claims.scope: pollen grains of angiosperms and spores of ferns and red algae formed in tetrads
measurable_quantities: timing of wall hardening relative to tetrad separation
claims.candidate_data: Palynological image databases (e.g. PalDat) of pollen morphology combined with developmental studies of tetrad separation timing.

claims.label: Outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells
claims.claim: Because quadrangular cells subdivide by periclinal walls that strengthen the boundary while triangular cells divide by oblique anticlines, outward growth is greater over triangular cells, so buds and outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells, as is widely seen in cryptogams.
claims.quote: As a direct and immediate consequence of this we might expect a tendency for special outgrowths, or “buds,” to arise from the triangular rather than from the quadrangular cells; and this turns out to be not merely a tendency towards which theoretical considerations point, but a widespread and important factor in the morphology of the cryptogams.
claims.scope: growing points and buds of cryptogams (mosses, liverworts, ferns, algae)
measurable_quantities: shape of cells giving rise to buds
frequency of bud initiation by cell shape
claims.candidate_data: Published lineage studies of bud and branch initiation in moss protonemata and fern gametophytes; no dedicated database known.

claims.section: Growth rate and plane of division
claims.label: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claims.claim: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.
claims.quote: the manner in which this latter cell divides will simply depend upon the form it has assumed before each successive act of division takes place, that is to say upon the ratio between its rate of growth and the frequency of its successive divisions.
claims.scope: apical and growing cells of mosses, liverworts, ferns and algae
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse imaging of moss protonemata and apical cells (e.g. published Physcomitrium growth studies) giving growth rates and division planes.

claims.label: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass
claims.claim: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.
claims.quote: The complex cell-network is not the cause but the result of the general configuration, which latter has its essential cause in whatsoever physical and chemical processes have led to a varying velocity of growth in one direction as compared with another.
claims.scope: growing multicellular plant and animal structures
claims.candidate_data: Published time-lapse growth-tracking datasets of plant organs and mutants with altered cell division but normal shape (e.g. lineage-tracked shoot apex and leaf datasets).

claims.label: Skeletal salts precipitate in dead or inactive matrix, not living protoplasm
claims.claim: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.
claims.quote: for the actual _precipitation_ takes place, as a rule, not in actively living, but in dead or at least inactive tissue: that is to say in the “formed material” or matrix which (as for instance in cartilage) accumulates round the living cells
claims.scope: calcified and silicified skeletal elements of animals and plants (spicules, concretions, cartilage and bone)
measurable_quantities: location of mineral nucleation sites relative to cells
claims.candidate_data: Published electron-microscopy and correlative imaging studies of biomineralisation sites (e.g. matrix vesicles in cartilage, sponge sclerocytes), including image sets in the Image Data Resource or EMPIAR.

claims.label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms
claims.claim: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.
claims.quote: the eggs of sea-urchins reared in lime-free water develop in apparent health, into larvae entirely destitute of the usual skeleton of calcareous rods, and in which, accordingly, the long arms of the Pluteus larva, which the rods support and distend, are entirely suppressed.
claims.scope: echinoid pluteus larvae (and by extension skeleton-forming organisms deprived of skeletal material)
claims.candidate_data: Published sea-urchin larval culture experiments under low-calcium and ocean-acidification conditions, many with data deposited on Dryad or PANGAEA.

claims.label: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight
claims.claim: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.
claims.quote: an example limited but yet crucial (_if confirmed_), of an asymmetric force, non-vital in its origin, which might conceivably be the starting-point of that asymmetry which is characteristic of so many organic products.
claims.scope: optically active (chiral) compounds produced by living organisms; origin of biological homochirality
measurable_quantities: enantiomeric excess produced by circularly polarised light photolysis
claims.candidate_data: Laboratory photochemistry studies of enantiomeric excess under circularly polarised light, and enantiomeric analyses of amino acids in carbonaceous meteorites.

claims.label: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites
claims.claim: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.
claims.quote: The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith of a mollusc or of a bony fish.
claims.scope: pearls, molluscan and teleost otoliths, and similar calcareous concretions
claims.candidate_data: Published microstructural (SEM, EBSD) studies of otoliths and pearls compared with biomimetic calcium carbonate precipitates in protein gels.

claims.label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons
claims.claim: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.
claims.quote: it is at least obvious, with the Liesegang phenomenon in view, that we have no right to _assume_ that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily bound up with, and indubitably brought about by, a periodic recurrence of particular _external_ conditions.
claims.scope: fish scales and otoliths, bones, starch grains and other concentrically zoned organic structures
measurable_quantities: number of otolith or scale zones
claims.candidate_data: Otolith age-validation studies using known-age or marked fish and bomb-radiocarbon dating, including deep-sea species; fisheries otolith archives.

claims.section: Solubility of calcium salts in colloids
claims.label: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down
claims.claim: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
claims.quote: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.
claims.scope: calcified tissues of animals, especially bone and calcareous skeletons
measurable_quantities: solubility of calcium salts in protein solutions vs. protein hydrolysates
claims.candidate_data: Published physical-chemistry measurements of calcium phosphate and carbonate solubility in the presence of proteins and peptides, and studies of protease activity at mineralisation fronts.

claims.section: Classification of skeletal forms by scale
claims.label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics
claims.claim: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.
claims.quote: The effect of _scale_, then, of which we had so much to say in our introductory chapter on Magnitude, is bound to be apparent in the study of skeletal fabrics, and to lead to essential differences between the big and the little, the massive and the minute, in regard to their controlling forces and their resultant forms.
claims.scope: skeletal elements of all sizes, from protist skeletons and spicules to vertebrate bones
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Spicules confined to a cell surface
claims.label: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic
claims.claim: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.
claims.notation: spicule follows a geodesic of the cell surface: \kappa_g = 0
claims.quote: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.
claims.scope: small curved intracellular spicules of sponges and holothurians (sigmata, amphidiscs and similar)
measurable_quantities: shape and axes of the sclerocyte
spicule orientation relative to cell axes
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT and SEM image sets of sponge spicules (e.g. in MorphoSource) and published sclerocyte imaging studies.

claims.section: Spicules confined to a cell surface
claims.label: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry
claims.claim: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.
claims.quote: the Holothurian spicules are composed of calcium carbonate while those which we have just described in the case of sponges are usually, if not always, siliceous: this being just another proof of the fact that in such cases the form of the spicule is not due to its chemical nature or molecular structure, but to the external forces
claims.scope: sponge and holothurian spicules
measurable_quantities: spicule shape descriptors in sponges and holothurians
claims.candidate_data: Comparative morphometric data from spicule image collections (e.g. MorphoSource, museum SEM archives) and the World Porifera Database for taxonomic context.

claims.label: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°
claims.claim: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.
claims.notation: three equal cells \Rightarrow triradiate spicule, rays at 120^\circ; four cells \Rightarrow tetraradiate, rays at \approx 109^\circ 28'
claims.quote: It is plain, accordingly, that in any flattened or stratified assemblage of such cells, a solidified skeletal deposit which originates or accumulates either between the cells or within the thickness of their mutual partitions, will tend to take the form of triradiate bodies, whose rays (in a typical case) will be set at equal angles of 120°
claims.scope: triradiate and tetractinellid spicules of calcareous and tetractinellid sponges
measurable_quantities: size and arrangement of surrounding cells or chambers
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT and SEM spicule images (e.g. MorphoSource) and published developmental imaging of calcareous sponge spicule formation by sclerocytes.

claims.label: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles
claims.claim: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.
claims.quote: the cells or vesicles by which they are conformed are not arranged in what is known as “closest packing,” but in linear series; so that in their arrangement, and by their mutual compression, we tend to get a pattern, not of hexagons, but of squares: or, looking to the solid, not of dodecahedra but of cubes or parallelopipeda.
claims.scope: hexactinellid (glass) sponges
measurable_quantities: spatial arrangement of chambers or syncytial units around forming spicules
claims.candidate_data: Published histological and 3D imaging studies of hexactinellid tissue and spicule formation.

claims.label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally
claims.claim: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.
claims.quote: the distribution of species in space is curious and vague; many species are found all over the world, or at least every here and there, with no evidence of specific limitations of geographical habitat
claims.scope: Radiolaria, living and fossil
measurable_quantities: geographic range sizes of radiolarian species
species richness and dominance per sample
stratigraphic ranges of genera and families
claims.candidate_data: Radiolarian occurrence data in GBIF, the Paleobiology Database and the Neptune microfossil database; plankton net and sediment-trap census counts.

claims.label: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill
claims.claim: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.
claims.quote: The formation of an “agglutinated” shell is thus seen to be a purely physical phenomenon, and indeed a special case of a more general physical phenomenon which has many other important consequences in biology.
claims.scope: agglutinated testate amoebae and foraminifera
claims.candidate_data: Published experiments on testate amoeba and agglutinated foraminifera grain selection, and sediment-versus-test grain composition studies.

claims.label: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles
claims.claim: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give concentric shells.
claims.quote: it will at once follow that they will show a tendency to aggregate in the grooves which separate the vesicles, and the result will be the development of a most delicate sphere composed of tiny rods arranged in a regular hexagonal network
claims.scope: spherical lattice-shelled Radiolaria (e.g. Aulonia, Actinomma, Cenosphaera)
measurable_quantities: mesh polygon size distribution and side number
claims.candidate_data: SEM image collections of radiolarian shells and published live-cell imaging of radiolarian cytoplasm and skeletogenesis.

claims.label: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles
claims.claim: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.
claims.quote: This is only another proof (if proof be needed) that the peculiar conformation of these little skeletons is not due to the material of which they are composed, but to the moulding of that material upon an underlying vesicular structure.
claims.scope: Radiolaria and Heliozoa with lattice skeletons of different composition
measurable_quantities: mesh regularity of shells of different composition
claims.candidate_data: Comparative SEM images of siliceous radiolarians, acantharians and Clathrulina from museum and published collections.

claims.label: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells
claims.claim: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.
claims.notation: six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120^\circ; edges meeting at \approx 109^\circ 28'
claims.quote: It is obvious at a glance that this is such a skeleton as may have been formed (I think we may go so far as to say _must_ have been formed) at the interfaces of a little tetrahedral group of cells
claims.scope: Nassellaria with tetrahedral skeletons (e.g. Callimitra)
measurable_quantities: angles between skeletal plates and edges
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT or SEM reconstructions of nassellarian skeletons and published studies of radiolarian skeletogenesis.

claims.label: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning
claims.claim: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.
claims.quote: If we may safely judge from Haeckel’s figures, the pentagonal dodecahedron of the Radiolarian is perfectly regular, and we must presume, accordingly, that it is not brought about by principles of space-partitioning similar to those which manifest themselves in the phenomenon of crystallisation.
claims.scope: polyhedral Radiolaria (Circoporidae and allies)
measurable_quantities: vertex angles and face regularity of polyhedral shells
number and positions of radial spines
claims.candidate_data: 3D reconstructions (micro-CT, SEM tilt series) of polyhedral radiolarian shells from museum collections.

claims.label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement
claims.claim: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.
claims.quote: The true symmetry of this figure, then, is hexagonal, with a polar axis, produced into two polar spicules; with six equatorial spicules, or rays; and with two sets of six spicular rays, interposed between the polar axis and the equatorial rays, and alternating in position with the latter.
claims.scope: Acantharia and allied Radiolaria with twenty radial spines (e.g. Dorataspis, Phatnaspis)
measurable_quantities: angular positions (latitude and longitude) of the twenty spines
claims.candidate_data: 3D imaging of acantharian skeletons and published spine-geometry measurements of Acantharia.

claims.label: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics
claims.claim: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.
claims.quote: But there are no obvious mechanical forces by which we can so explain this peculiar polarity. This at least is evident, that it arises in the central mass of protoplasm, which is the essential living portion of the organism
claims.scope: Radiolaria with fixed numbers and positions of radial spines (Acantharia, Phaeodaria)
measurable_quantities: site of spine initiation relative to central capsule
spine arrangement in early developmental stages
claims.candidate_data: Published developmental and cytological studies of acantharian spine formation.

claims.label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics
claims.claim: The three kinds of geodetic on a cylinder (parallel rings, straight longitudinal lines and helical spirals) are all realised in the local wall thickenings of cylindrical plant cells and vessels, and the helical geodetic in the spiral coils of insect tracheae and tracheids.
claims.notation: geodesics on a cylinder of radius r: circles z = c, lines \theta = c, helices z = a\theta
claims.quote: These three systems are all of frequent occurrence, and are all illustrated in the local thickenings of the wall of the cylindrical cells or vessels of plants.
