claims.scope: plant xylem vessels and tracheids, insect tracheae
measurable_quantities: orientation and pitch of wall thickenings
claims.candidate_data: Plant anatomy image collections and published micro-CT of xylem secondary walls and insect tracheae.

claims.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
claims.claim: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.
claims.notation: spiral geodesic on a right cone (\kappa_g = 0) coils more closely as the cone narrows
claims.quote: In a right cone, the spiral geodetic falls into closer and closer coils as the diameter of the cone narrows; and a very beautiful geodetic of this kind is exemplified in the sutural line of a spiral shell, such as Turritella
claims.scope: high-spired gastropod shells (e.g. Turritella)
measurable_quantities: suture path on the shell surface
whorl spacing versus shell diameter along the spire
claims.candidate_data: 3D surface scans of gastropod shells in MorphoSource and museum collections.

claims.label: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns
claims.claim: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
claims.quote: and it is also common to find the two systems interfering with one another, and forming a criss-cross, or reticulated arrangement. This is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
claims.scope: reticulated patterns on cylindrical and curved organic surfaces (cell walls, integuments)
measurable_quantities: angles and geodesic deviation of the crossing pattern lines on the surface
claims.candidate_data: Image collections of reticulate cell-wall thickenings and other surface patterns; none specifically compiled.

claims.label: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves
claims.claim: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).
claims.notation: fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface takes the shortest path: \kappa_g = 0
claims.quote: Thus the muscular fibres, as they wind over the curved surface of an organ, arrange themselves automatically in geodesic curves: in precisely the same manner as we also automatically construct complex systems of geodesics whenever we wind a ball of wool or a spindle of tow
claims.scope: muscular walls of hollow and tubular organs (heart, stomach, blood vessels, gut, worm body wall)
measurable_quantities: 3D muscle fibre orientations on organ surfaces
geodesic paths on the reconstructed organ surface
claims.candidate_data: Diffusion-tensor MRI fibre-orientation atlases of the heart and gut, and published histological fibre-orientation maps.

claims.label: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube
claims.claim: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the shortest course.
claims.quote: these systems of muscular fibres, geodetic to begin with, remain geodetic (in the sense in which we are using the word) after all the twisting to which the primitive cylindrical tube or tubes have been subjected.
claims.scope: vertebrate (especially mammalian) heart and stomach musculature
measurable_quantities: deviation of fibre paths from surface geodesics
developmental fibre orientation in heart tube looping
claims.candidate_data: Cardiac diffusion-tensor MRI datasets and developmental imaging of heart-tube looping in model organisms.

claims.label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path
claims.claim: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.
claims.quote: And this axial rotation, just as in the case of a rifle-bullet, causes their natural swerve, which is always in the same direction as regards their own bodies, to be in a continually changing direction as regards space: in short, to make a spiral course around, and more or less approximate to, a straight axial line.
claims.scope: ciliates, flagellates, rotifers, swarm-spores and other small swimming organisms
measurable_quantities: helix radius and pitch of swimming trajectories
claims.candidate_data: Published 3D tracking datasets of microorganism swimming trajectories (e.g. on Dryad or Zenodo).

claims.label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral
claims.claim: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.
claims.notation: r = a e^{\theta \cot\alpha}
claims.quote: Of the spiral forms which we have now mentioned, every one (with the single exception of the outline of the cordate leaf) is an example of the remarkable curve known as the Logarithmic Spiral.
claims.scope: ruminant horns, molluscan shells, foraminiferal shells, sunflower capitula; excludes cordate leaf outlines
measurable_quantities: polar radius as a function of vectorial angle
goodness of fit of logarithmic versus other spiral models
claims.candidate_data: 3D surface scans and CT images of shells and horns from MorphoSource, and published sunflower capitulum images, fitted with spiral models.

claims.label: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one
claims.claim: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle does in the snail-shell.
claims.quote: the growing curve will tend to wind round and round its point of origin. In the typical case of the snail-shell, such an intrinsic force is manifestly present in the action of the columellar muscle.
claims.scope: spirally growing shells and other growing structures subject to deflecting forces
measurable_quantities: shell coiling direction relative to gravity
claims.candidate_data: Studies of gastropod shell coiling under altered orientation or microgravity and anatomical data on columellar muscle; none known as a dedicated dataset.

claims.label: A constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates yields a logarithmic spiral
claims.claim: In a tubular structure whose growth is unequal on its two sides, a constant ratio between the rates of growth in the longitudinal and transverse directions generally produces a logarithmic spiral, the value of the ratio fixing the spiral's constant angle, with the circle and the straight line as limiting cases.
claims.notation: constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates \Rightarrow r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}, the ratio fixing \alpha; \alpha = 90^\circ circle, \alpha \to 0 straight line
claims.quote: In other words, in such a structure as we have presupposed, the existence or maintenance of a constant ratio between the rates of extension or growth in the vertical and transverse directions will lead, in general, to the development of a logarithmic spiral; the magnitude of that ratio will determine the character (that is to say, the constant angle) of the spiral;
claims.scope: tubular shells and horns growing by unequal accretion
measurable_quantities: growth rate at outer versus inner margin of the aperture
claims.candidate_data: Sclerochronological growth-increment measurements on shells and horn growth-ring data, combined with spiral-angle measurements from CT scans (e.g. MorphoSource).

claims.label: The scorpioid cyme traces a true logarithmic spiral
claims.claim: In a scorpioid cyme, where each shoot arises from the last on the same side at an equal angle and successive shoots diminish in length in a constant ratio, the shoots are tangents to a true logarithmic spiral; in the helicoid cyme the same spiral is present but hidden by a superimposed twist.
claims.notation: successive shoots l_{n+1} = q\,l_n at equal angles are tangents to r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}
claims.quote: The result is that the successive shoots, or successive increments of growth, are tangents to a curve, and this curve is a true logarithmic spiral.
claims.scope: scorpioid and helicoid (cymose) inflorescences, e.g. borage
claims.candidate_data: Herbarium specimen images (e.g. via GBIF) and plant architecture measurements of Boraginaceae inflorescences.

claims.label: The shell grows in size without changing its shape
claims.claim: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.
claims.notation: r(\theta + \phi) = e^{\phi\cot\alpha}\,r(\theta): rotation by \phi equals scaling, so shape is invariant under terminal growth
claims.quote: The shell, like the creature within it, grows in size _but does not change its shape_; and the existence of this constant relativity of growth, or constant similarity of form, is of the essence, and may be made the basis of a definition, of the logarithmic spiral.
claims.scope: molluscan shells, horns and other structures growing by terminal accretion
measurable_quantities: shape descriptors of juvenile versus adult shells
spiral parameters measured at different growth stages
claims.candidate_data: Ontogenetic series of shell CT scans or images (MorphoSource, museum collections) analysed with geometric morphometrics.

claims.label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it
claims.claim: In horns, shells and all other organic forms showing a logarithmic spiral, the existing structure is partly old and partly new, and each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the whole pre-existing structure, that is, an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before.
claims.notation: each increment G is a gnomon: F \cup G \sim F
claims.quote: (2) it is characteristic of the growth of the horn, of the shell, and of all other organic forms in which a logarithmic spiral can be recognised, that _each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the entire pre-existing structure_.
claims.scope: molluscan shells and opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns, tusks
measurable_quantities: shape of successive growth increments or chambers
similarity of whole structure before and after each increment
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT chamber-by-chamber reconstructions of foraminifera and cephalopod shells (e.g. MorphoSource) and horn growth-ring images.

claims.label: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts
claims.claim: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.
claims.quote: For it follows as a simple corollary to this theorem of gnomons that we must not expect to find the logarithmic spiral manifested in a structure whose parts are simultaneously produced, as for instance in the margin of a leaf, or among the many curves that make the contour of a fish.
claims.scope: organic curves in general; accretionary hard parts versus soft tissues and leaf margins
measurable_quantities: fit of logarithmic spiral to organic outlines
claims.candidate_data: Outline and surface datasets of shells, horns and claws (MorphoSource) compared with leaf-outline and fish-shape image datasets.

claims.section: Measuring the spiral of the shell
claims.label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression
claims.claim: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).
claims.notation: whorl breadths b_{n+1}/b_n = \text{const} = e^{2\pi\cot\alpha}; Nautilus \approx 3
claims.quote: It was by observing, with the help of very careful measurement, this continued proportionality, that Moseley was enabled to verify his first assumption, based on the general appearance of the shell, that the shell of Nautilus was actually a logarithmic spiral, and this demonstration he was immediately afterwards in a position to generalise by extending it to all the spiral Ammonitoid and Gastropod mollusca
claims.scope: Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropod shells
measurable_quantities: breadths of successive whorls along a radius vector
claims.candidate_data: Published whorl-expansion-rate measurements of ammonoids and gastropods, and shell CT scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios
claims.claim: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative magnitudes of these factors.
claims.quote: In short it is obvious that _all_ the differences of form which we observe between one shell and another are referable to matters of _degree_, depending, one and all, upon the relative magnitudes of the various factors in the complex equation to the curve.
claims.scope: univalve (discoid and turbinate) molluscan shells
measurable_quantities: distance of generating curve from axis
claims.candidate_data: Theoretical-morphospace analyses of real shells using Raupian coiling parameters, fitted to shell scans from MorphoSource or museum image collections.

claims.label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°
claims.claim: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.
claims.notation: \alpha \approx 80^\circ in Nautilus (b_{n+1}/b_n \approx 3); usually 80^\circ \le \alpha \le 85^\circ in ammonitoid and gastropod shells
claims.quote: the constant angle is in the neighbourhood of 80°; and hence also that, in all the ordinary Ammonitoid shells, and in all the typically spiral shells of the Gastropods, the constant angle is also a large one, being very seldom less than 80°, and usually between 80° and 85°.
claims.scope: Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropods
measurable_quantities: ratio of breadths of successive whorls
claims.candidate_data: Published Raupian coiling-parameter (whorl expansion rate) compilations for ammonoids and gastropods, and MorphoSource shell scans.

claims.label: Separation or overlap of whorls reflects the growth-rate ratio of outer to inner border
claims.claim: Whether the whorls of a spiral shell stand apart, just touch, or overlap (up to complete involution, as in Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus) depends only on the ratio of the rate of growth of the outer border of the tube to that of its inner border.
claims.quote: For the purposes of the morphologist, then, the main result of this last general investigation is to shew that all the various types of “open” and “closed” spirals, all the various degrees of separation or overlap of the successive whorls, are simply the outward expression of a varying ratio in the _rate of growth_ of the outer as compared with the inner border of the tubular shell.
claims.scope: discoid and turbinate molluscan shells, including nautiloids and ammonoids
measurable_quantities: inner versus outer whorl radius on the same radius vector
degree of whorl overlap or umbilical width
claims.candidate_data: Ammonoid and nautiloid coiling-parameter datasets (whorl overlap, umbilical ratio) and shell CT scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry
claims.claim: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.
claims.quote: _To such phylogenetic hypotheses the mathematical or dynamical study of the forms of shells lends no valid support._ If we have two shells in which the constant angle of the spire be respectively 80° and 60°, that fact in itself does not at all justify an assertion that the one is more primitive, more ancient, or more “ancestral” than the other.
claims.scope: cephalopod (nautiloid and ammonoid) shell forms and phylogenetic inference from them
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence ages combined with cephalopod coiling-parameter datasets and published cephalopod phylogenies.

claims.label: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence
claims.claim: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.
claims.quote: And to my mind, the mathematical (as distinguished from the purely physical) study of morphology bids fair to help us to recognise this phenomenon of orthogenesis in many cases where it is not at once patent to the eye; and also, on the other hand, to warn us, in many other cases, that even strong and apparently complex resemblances in form may be capable of arising independently,
claims.scope: fossil and living lineages, especially molluscan shells
measurable_quantities: frequency of convergent shell forms across clades
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database stratigraphic data combined with shell morphometrics, and phylogenies for convergence analysis.

claims.section: Changes of spiral angle with age
claims.label: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites
claims.claim: In some ammonoids the spiral angle changes progressively during growth: where it increases the whorls become narrower (as in Oekotraustes), and where it diminishes towards zero the coil opens out into an almost straight curve (as in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites).
claims.quote: But let us suppose that the spiral angle increases somewhat rapidly; we shall then get a spiral with gradually narrowing whorls, and this condition is characteristic of Oekotraustes, a subgenus of Ammonites. If on the other hand, the angle α gradually diminishes, and even falls away to zero, we shall have the spiral curve opening out, as it does in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites,
claims.scope: ammonoids and nautiloids with changing coiling (e.g. Oekotraustes, Scaphites, Ancyloceras, Lituites)
measurable_quantities: spiral angle or whorl expansion rate as a function of whorl number
claims.candidate_data: Ontogenetic coiling measurements of heteromorph ammonoids from published morphometric studies and MorphoSource fossil scans.

claims.label: Dissimilar turbinate shells share similar spiral angles and differ mainly in apical angle
claims.claim: Shells as different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little in their spiral angle (the ratio of radial to tangential growth) and differ in form mainly in the apical angle of the enveloping cone, which is set by the rate of translation along the axis relative to growth.
claims.quote: We see from this that shells so different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little indeed in the magnitude of the spiral angle α, that is to say in the relative velocities of radial and tangential growth. It is upon the angle θ that the difference in their form mainly depends:
claims.scope: turbinate and discoid gastropod shells
measurable_quantities: apical semi-angle of the enveloping cone
ratio of breadths of successive whorls
claims.candidate_data: Gastropod shell morphometric datasets with coiling parameters (whorl expansion rate and translation rate) and shell scans in MorphoSource.

claims.label: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate
claims.claim: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures (as in Lima or Solen).
claims.notation: r(\theta, t) = t\,f(\theta) from the umbo; f(\theta) = \cos\theta gives coaxial circles
claims.quote: All that we are immediately concerned with is the simple fact that where a velocity, such as our rate of growth, varies with its direction,—varies that is to say as a function of the angular divergence from a certain axis,—then, in a certain simple case, we get lines of growth laid down as a system of coaxial circles,
claims.scope: lamellibranch and brachiopod shells with visible growth lines
measurable_quantities: radial growth increment as a function of direction from the umbo
claims.candidate_data: Outline and growth-line images of bivalve shells from museum collections and sclerochronology studies; elliptic Fourier outline datasets.

claims.label: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines
claims.claim: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.
claims.quote: But in Estheria (and one or two other small crustacea) the moult is incomplete: the old carapace is retained, and the new, growing up underneath it, adheres to it like a lining, and projects beyond its edge: so that in course of time the margins of successive old carapaces appear as “lines of growth” upon the surface of the shell.
claims.scope: Estheria and similar conchostracan crustaceans
measurable_quantities: number of growth lines versus number of moults
claims.candidate_data: Published morphometric studies of clam shrimp (Spinicaudata) carapace growth lines and museum specimen images.

claims.label: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint
claims.claim: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.
claims.quote: It is obvious that the incipient curvature of the arms, and consequently the form and direction of the spirals, will be influenced by the surrounding pressures, and these in turn by the general shape of the shell. We shall expect, accordingly, to find the long outwardly directed spirals associated with shells which are transversely elongated, as Spirifer is; while the more rounded Atrypas will tend to the opposite condition.
claims.scope: spire-bearing brachiopods (Spiriferida, Atrypida, Athyridida and others)
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database brachiopod occurrences with shell-shape measurements and published serial-section or CT reconstructions of brachidia.

claims.label: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone
claims.claim: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.
claims.quote: In short, I think there is reason to believe, or at least to suspect, that we have in the shell and Aptychus of the Ammonites, two portions of a once united structure; of which other Cephalopods retain not both parts but only one or other, one as the ventrally situated shell of Nautilus, the other as the dorsally placed shell for example of Sepia or of Spirula.
claims.scope: ammonoids, Nautilus, Sepia, Spirula and other cephalopods; thecosome pteropods
measurable_quantities: developmental origin of aptychi and cephalopod shells
homology of dorsal and ventral shell fields
claims.candidate_data: Developmental and histological studies of cephalopod shell fields and ammonoid aptychi, and molecular phylogenies of Cephalopoda; none known as a dedicated dataset.

claims.label: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films
claims.claim: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.
claims.quote: In all cases, provided only that the membrane be isotropic, the form assumed will be precisely that of a soap-bubble under similar conditions of attachment: that is to say, it will be (with the usual limitations or conditions) a surface of minimal area.
claims.scope: septa of nautiloid, orthocone and ammonoid shells
measurable_quantities: mean curvature constancy across the septum
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT reconstructions of Nautilus and ammonoid septa (e.g. MorphoSource) analysed for mean curvature.

claims.label: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon
claims.claim: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.
claims.quote: Superposed upon the usual sinuous outline, with its “lobes” and “saddles,” we have here a minutely ramified, or arborescent outline, in which all the branches terminate in wavy, more or less circular arcs,—looking just like the ‘landscape marble’ from the Bristol Rhaetic. We have no difficulty in recognising in this a surface-tension phenomenon.
claims.scope: ammonoids with complex (ammonitic) suture lines
measurable_quantities: fractal dimension or complexity of suture lines
claims.candidate_data: Published ammonoid suture-complexity (fractal dimension) datasets and digitised suture lines, compared with viscous-fingering patterns.

claims.label: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas
claims.claim: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.
claims.quote: Again, we find the same forms, or forms which (save for external ornament) are mathematically identical, repeating themselves in all periods of the world’s geological history; and, irrespective of climate or local conditions, we see them mixed up, one with another, in the depths and on the shores of every sea.
claims.scope: spiral shells of molluscs, foraminifera and tube-dwelling worms through geological time
measurable_quantities: coiling parameters by clade, geological period and environment
claims.candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences with environment and age, combined with shell coiling-parameter datasets and OBIS/GBIF distribution records.

claims.label: Natural Selection plays no necessary part in producing spiral shell forms
claims.claim: Natural Selection, in any strictly biological sense, has no necessary share in producing the varied forms of spiral shells, which arise from differences in growth rates and ratios.
claims.quote: It is hard indeed (to my mind) to see where Natural Selection necessarily enters in, or to admit that it has had any share whatsoever in the production of these varied conformations.
claims.scope: spiral shells of molluscs, foraminifera and worms
measurable_quantities: association between coiling parameters and fitness or ecological performance
shell-form disparity relative to adaptive expectations
claims.candidate_data: Functional-morphology and hydrodynamic studies of shell coiling, with Paleobiology Database survivorship data; none known that directly settles the question.

claims.label: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension
claims.claim: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.
claims.quote: wherever the shell is but a single unit or single chamber, its form may be explained in general by the laws of surface tension: the assumption being that the little mass of protoplasm which makes the simple shell behaves as a _fluid drop_, the form of which is perpetuated when the protoplasm acquires its solid covering.
claims.scope: unilocular Foraminifera (e.g. Orbulina, Lagena)
claims.candidate_data: 3D micro-CT and image collections of foraminiferal tests such as the Endless Forams image set and MorphoSource scans, compared with computed drop shapes.

claims.label: Foraminifera are spiral because they grow by permanent increments added outside
claims.claim: Foraminiferal shells tend towards a spiral form because they grow by successive increments added to the exterior, each of which becomes a permanent, rigid part of the structure.
claims.quote: That the shell in the Foraminifera should tend towards a spiral form need not surprise us; for we have learned that one of the fundamental conditions of the production of a concrete spiral is just precisely what we have here, namely the gradual development of a structure by means of successive increments superadded to its exterior, which then form part, successively, of a permanent and rigid structure.
claims.scope: multilocular Foraminifera, contrasted with Radiolaria
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT ontogenetic reconstructions of foraminiferal tests published on MorphoSource and Dryad.

claims.label: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side
claims.claim: Foraminiferal septa are convex outwards and those of Nautilus concave outwards because the pressure each membrane resisted when it set lay on opposite sides; in both cases the septum tends to a surface of minimal area.
claims.quote: The one septum is, speaking generally, the reverse of the other; the organism, so to speak, is outside the one and inside the other; and in both cases alike, the septum tends to assume the form of a surface of minimal area, as permitted, or as defined, by all the circumstances of the case.
claims.scope: septa of chambered Foraminifera and chambered cephalopod shells
measurable_quantities: sign and magnitude of septal curvature
septal surface area relative to bounding contour
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT scans of foraminifera and Nautilus shells on MorphoSource.

claims.label: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones
claims.claim: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.
claims.notation: r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}, recognised by self-similarity of young and old shells
claims.quote: The logarithmic spiral is easily recognisable in typical cases (and especially where the spire makes more than one visible revolution about the pole), by its fundamental property of continued similarity: that is to say, by reason of the fact that the big many-chambered shell is of just the same shape as the smaller and younger shell
claims.scope: nautiloid and other spiral Foraminifera
measurable_quantities: radius of successive whorls versus vectorial angle
shape of juvenile versus adult test
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT data of planispiral and trochospiral foraminifera on MorphoSource; published chamber-by-chamber morphometric datasets on Dryad.

claims.label: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°
claims.claim: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.
claims.notation: Fusulina: b_{n+1}/b_n \approx 1.5 \Rightarrow \alpha \approx 86^\circ
claims.quote: And this ratio of 1·5 between the breadths of successive whorls corresponds (as we see by our table on p. 534) to a constant angle of about 86°, or just such a spiral as we commonly meet with in the Ammonites
claims.scope: fusulinid Foraminifera (Fusulina cylindrica, F. Böcki)
claims.candidate_data: Thin-section morphometric data on fusulinids in the paleontological literature and specimen records in the Paleobiology Database.

claims.label: Constant chamber-size ratio follows from growth proportional to existing mass
claims.claim: Each foraminiferal chamber bears a constant ratio of size to the next because the rate of increase at each instant is proportional to the whole existing mass of the homogeneous organism.
claims.notation: dM/dt \propto M \Rightarrow V_{n+1}/V_n = \text{const}
claims.quote: The law of increase by which each chamber bears a constant ratio of magnitude to the next may be looked upon as a simple consequence of the structural uniformity or homogeneity of the organism; we have merely to suppose (as this uniformity would naturally lead us to do) that the rate of increase is at each instant proportional to the whole existing mass.
claims.scope: chambered Foraminifera
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT chamber volume series for planktonic foraminifera published on Dryad and MorphoSource.

claims.label: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral
claims.claim: Each new protoplasmic drop settles in a position of minimum potential energy (including minimal area), which makes each chamber similar to the last; proportional growth of size then gives the series the form of a logarithmic spiral. Rhumbler's specific 'law of the constant angle' of contact is too narrow an explanation.
claims.quote: The physical law of minimum potential (including also the law of minimal area) is all that we need in order to explain, _in general terms_, the continued similarity of one chamber to another; and the physiological law of growth, by which a continued proportionality of size tends to run through the series of successive chambers, impresses upon this series of similar increments the form of a logarithmic spiral.
claims.scope: chambered Foraminifera
claims.candidate_data: Micro-CT chamber reconstructions of foraminifera compared with physical simulations of sequential drop accretion.

claims.label: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side
claims.claim: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.
claims.quote: The majority of spiral forms, on the other hand, are plane or discoid spirals, and we may take it that in these cases some force has exercised a controlling influence, so as to keep all the chambers in a plane. This is especially the case in forms like Rotalia or Discorbina (Fig. 316), where the organism lives attached to a rock or a frond of sea-weed
claims.scope: benthic attached versus planktonic Foraminifera
claims.candidate_data: Foraminiferal trait compilations (life habit and coiling mode) such as the Triton planktonic foraminifera dataset and the World Foraminifera Database.

claims.section: Variability and the constancy of species
claims.label: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability
claims.claim: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.
claims.quote: but for all we know of the life-history of the Foraminifera, it may well be that a great number of the other forms which we distinguish as separate species and even genera are no more than temporary manifestations of the same variability
claims.scope: Foraminifera, especially Peneroplis
measurable_quantities: ecophenotypic response of shell form to environment
claims.candidate_data: Molecular barcoding studies of foraminiferal morphospecies (e.g. the PFR2 Planktonic Foraminifera Ribosomal Reference database) and culture experiments on ecophenotypic variation.

claims.label: Foraminiferal forms follow such simple laws that none is fitter than another to survive
claims.claim: Foraminiferal shells grow by laws so simple and so in harmony with their material and the forces acting on them that no form is better, fitter or less fit to survive than another, which accounts for the great diversity of types and their persistence since the Cretaceous.
claims.quote: It leads one to imagine that these shells have grown according to laws so simple, so much in harmony with their material, with their environment, and with all the forces internal and external to which they are exposed, that none is better than another and none fitter or less fit to survive.
claims.scope: Foraminifera
measurable_quantities: relationship between test morphology and extinction or survival
claims.candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data for foraminifera in the Paleobiology Database and the Neptune (NSB) database, linked to morphological traits.

claims.label: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again
claims.claim: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.
claims.quote: It invites one also to contemplate the possibility of the lines of possible variation being here so narrow and determinate that identical forms may have come independently into being again and again.
claims.scope: Foraminifera through geological time
measurable_quantities: frequency of homeomorphy between unrelated lineages
claims.candidate_data: Morphology-calibrated phylogenies of planktonic foraminifera (e.g. Aze et al. 2011 Macroperforate phylogeny), the Triton dataset and molecular phylogenies.

claims.section: Strength as a supposed selective factor
claims.label: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution
claims.claim: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.
claims.quote: And so I am not inclined to believe that niceties of form affect the case very much: nor in general that foraminiferal life involves a struggle for existence wherein breakage is a constant danger to be averted, and increased strength an advantage to be ensured.
claims.scope: Foraminifera
measurable_quantities: breakage frequency of tests in death assemblages
mechanical strength of tests of differing complexity
claims.candidate_data: Taphonomic fragmentation studies of foraminiferal assemblages and mechanical testing studies of tests (e.g. finite-element analyses published on Dryad).

claims.section: Strength as a supposed selective factor
claims.label: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents
claims.claim: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.
claims.quote: The coarseness or fineness of the sediment on the sea-bottom is a measure of the current: where the current is strong the larger stones are washed clean, where there is perfect stillness the finest mud settles down; and the light, fragile shells of the Foraminifera find their appropriate place, like every other graded sediment, in this spontaneous order of lixiviation.
claims.scope: foraminiferal shells in marine sediments
claims.candidate_data: Seafloor sediment surveys with grain size and foraminiferal counts (e.g. the ForCenS census database and PANGAEA sediment datasets).

claims.label: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity
claims.claim: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.
claims.quote: But in so far as forms can be shewn to depend on the play of physical forces, and the variations of form to be directly due to simple quantitative variations in these, just so far are we thrown back on our guard before the biological conception of consanguinity, and compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny.
claims.scope: Foraminifera and other organisms whose form is governed by physical forces
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio
claims.claim: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.
claims.notation: v_{ant}/v_{post} = \text{const} \Rightarrow plane spiral r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}
claims.quote: Its longitudinal growth proceeds with a maximum velocity anteriorly, and a minimum posteriorly; and the ratio of these velocities being constant, the horn curves into the form of a logarithmic spiral in the manner that we have already studied.
claims.scope: rhinoceros horns
measurable_quantities: anterior and posterior horn growth rates
claims.candidate_data: 3D scans of rhinoceros skulls and horns on MorphoSource and museum specimen measurements.

claims.label: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
claims.claim: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.
claims.quote: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.
claims.scope: sheep, goats, oxen and antelopes (Bovidae)
measurable_quantities: handedness of left and right horns
claims.candidate_data: 3D surface scans of bovid skulls and horns on MorphoSource.

claims.label: Most horns are logarithmic spirals from constant unequal growth on opposite sides
claims.claim: In the great majority of horns the curve is a continuous logarithmic spiral, caused by unequal rates of growth parallel to the axis on opposite sides of the horn, the inequality keeping a constant ratio throughout growth.
claims.notation: v_1/v_2 = \text{const} on opposite sides of the axis \Rightarrow r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}
claims.quote: But in the great majority of horns, we have no difficulty in recognising a continuous logarithmic spiral, nor in referring it, as before, to an unequal rate of growth (parallel to the axis) on two opposite sides of the horn, the inequality maintaining a constant ratio as long as growth proceeds.
claims.scope: horns of hollow-horned ruminants
measurable_quantities: growth increments on inner and outer horn surfaces
claims.candidate_data: 3D horn scans on MorphoSource and published horn growth-ring measurements of wild sheep and goats.

claims.label: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle
claims.claim: Horns of wild goats and sheep form a series of homologous logarithmic spirals with increasing constant angle: under 40° in Oryx, under 70° in the Scinde wild goat, about 75° in Ovis ammon and a little more in the Highland ram.
claims.notation: \alpha < 40^\circ (Oryx), < 70^\circ (Scinde wild goat), \approx 75^\circ (Ovis ammon), > 75^\circ (Highland ram)
claims.quote: we may easily arrange a series of forms, such for example as the Siberian ibex, the moufflon, _Ovis Ammon_, etc., and ending with the long-horned Highland ram: in which, as we pass from one to another, we recognise precisely homologous spirals, with an increasing angular constant, the spiral angle being, for instance, about 75° or rather less in _Ovis Ammon_, and in the Highland ram a very little more.
claims.scope: horns of Oryx, Capra and Ovis species
measurable_quantities: logarithmic spiral constant angle of horns
claims.candidate_data: 3D horn scans of bovids on MorphoSource; published morphometric studies of caprine horn shape.

claims.label: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component
claims.claim: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.
claims.quote: In all of these the constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is very much the same, but the shearing component differs greatly.
claims.scope: Asiatic wild sheep (Ovis ammon, O. poli, O. hodgsoni)
measurable_quantities: helical pitch or translation per whorl
claims.candidate_data: 3D horn scans of Ovis species on MorphoSource and museum trophy measurements.

claims.label: A horn is a plane spiral only if fastest and slowest growth lie diametrically opposite
claims.claim: If the maximal and minimal growth rates around the basal growth zone of a horn lie diametrically opposite, the horn is a plane spiral; otherwise it is a spiral in space with a helical component, which is the usual case because the horn's field of force has no such plane of symmetry.
claims.notation: plane spiral iff the maximal and minimal growth rates around the base lie at \Delta\phi = 180^\circ; otherwise helicospiral
claims.quote: If the maximal and minimal velocities of growth be precisely at opposite sides of the zone of growth, the resultant spiral will be a plane spiral; but if they be not precisely or diametrically opposite, then the spiral will be a spiral in space, with a winding or helical component
claims.scope: horns of ruminants
measurable_quantities: circumferential distribution of growth rate at horn base
claims.candidate_data: Growth-ring and keratin deposition measurements on horns combined with 3D horn scans; none known as a ready dataset.

claims.label: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral
claims.claim: Unequal retardation of the growing horn sheath by its adhesion to the bony core can produce the same spiral as unequal growth, and is probably a very important and sometimes the chief factor in horn curvature.
claims.quote: had its elongation more retarded on one side than the other (prior to its complete solidification) by varying degrees of adhesion or membranous attachment to the bone core within, then the net result would be a spiral curve precisely such as would have arisen from initial inequalities in the rate of growth itself. It seems highly probable that this is a very important factor
claims.scope: horns of hollow-horned ruminants
measurable_quantities: sheath–core attachment strength around the circumference
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature
claims.claim: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.
claims.quote: I think it may be said that, on the whole, the thicker the horn, the greater is its spiral curvature.
claims.scope: horns of antelopes, goats and sheep
measurable_quantities: horn basal diameter or cross-sectional area
claims.candidate_data: 3D horn scans of bovids on MorphoSource and published bovid horn morphometric datasets.

claims.section: Torsion and growth lines of horns
claims.label: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain
claims.claim: Horns that grow as curves of double curvature undergo torsional strain, because the sheath is attached to the core, and this strain warps the rings into the sinuous growth lines predicted by St Venant for a twisted non-circular prism; such lines are absent from cylindrical ox horns.
claims.quote: But there is yet another and a very remarkable phenomenon which we may discern in the growth of a horn, when it takes the form of a curve of double curvature, namely, an effect of torsional strain; and this it is which gives rise to the sinuous “lines of growth,” or sinuous boundaries of the separate horny rings, of which we have already spoken.
claims.scope: horns of sheep, Ovis ammon, antelopes; contrasted with oxen
claims.candidate_data: 3D surface scans of horns on MorphoSource compared with elastic torsion models; no dedicated dataset known.

claims.label: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides
claims.claim: The revolving nutation of twining plants, like the helicoid growth of an antelope horn, is caused by unequal rates of growth on different sides of the stem, the difference being that in the stem growth occurs along its whole length.
claims.quote: This tendency to revolution—“circumvolution,” as Darwin calls it, “revolving nutation,” as Sachs puts it—is very closely comparable to the process by which an antelope’s horn (such as the koodoo’s) grows into its spiral or rather helicoid form; and it is simply due, in like manner, to inequalities in the rate of growth on different sides of the growing stem.
claims.scope: twining climbing plants
measurable_quantities: differential elongation rates around the stem circumference
claims.candidate_data: Time-lapse and kinematic studies of circumnutation in twining plants published in plant physiology literature.

claims.label: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation
claims.claim: Twining stems become twisted on rough supports but not on smooth ones because adhesion to the rough support sets up a mechanical couple, so Darwin's adaptive explanation (gaining rigidity) is unnecessary.
claims.quote: In the case of the roughened support, there is a temporary adhesion or “clinging” between it and the growing stem which twines around it; and a system of forces is thus set up, producing a “couple,” just as it was in the case of the ram’s or antelope’s horn through direct adhesion of the bony core to the surrounding sheath.
claims.scope: twining stems of climbing plants
claims.candidate_data: Experimental studies of twining on supports of differing roughness and diameter; none known as a dataset.

claims.label: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface
claims.claim: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.
claims.quote: The surface to which the branches of the antler tend to be confined is a more or less spheroidal, or occasionally an ellipsoidal one; and furthermore, when we inspect any well-developed pair of antlers, such as those of a red deer, a sambur or a wapiti, we have no difficulty in seeing that the two antlers make up between them _a single surface_
claims.scope: antlers of deer and elk (Cervidae)
measurable_quantities: 3D coordinates of beam and tine tips
deviation of tine positions from a fitted spheroid
claims.candidate_data: 3D scans of cervid skulls and antlers on MorphoSource; published antler morphometric datasets.

claims.label: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals
claims.claim: Wherever a structure grows by permanent increments with unequal longitudinal growth about its axis, as in nails, claws, beaks and teeth, it always tends to the form of a logarithmic spiral, which becomes conspicuous only when the structure is long.
claims.notation: unequal longitudinal growth by permanent increments \Rightarrow r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}
claims.quote: The logarithmic spiral _always_ tends to manifest itself in such structures as these, though it usually only attracts our attention in elongated structures, where (that is to say) the radius vector has described a considerable angle.
claims.scope: nails, claws, beaks, incisors, canines and tusks of vertebrates
measurable_quantities: curvature along the length of claw, beak or tooth
fit to logarithmic versus other spirals
claims.candidate_data: 3D scans of claws, beaks and teeth on MorphoSource; published claw curvature datasets for birds and squamates.

claims.label: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter
claims.claim: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.
claims.quote: but the American mastodons and the existing species of elephant have tusks which do not differ appreciably, except in size, from the great spiral tusks of the mammoth, though from their comparative shortness the spiral is little developed and only appears to the eye as a gentle curve.
claims.scope: tusks of elephants, mastodons and mammoths (Proboscidea)
claims.candidate_data: Museum collections and 3D scans of proboscidean tusks on MorphoSource; published tusk morphometric studies.

claims.section: Helices and logarithmic spirals in phyllotaxis
claims.label: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem
claims.claim: The logarithmic spirals of flat or convex inflorescences and the helices on elongated stems are one phenomenon: the fir-cone, teasel, thistle and sunflower heads are successive geometric deformations of a long, nearly cylindrical stem, on which the same arrangement appears as helices.
claims.quote: the semi-ellipsoidal capitulum of the teasel, the more or less hemispherical one of the thistle, and the flattened but still convex one of the sunflower, are all beautiful and successive deformations of what is typically a long, conical, and all but cylindrical stem.
claims.scope: leaf, scale and floret arrangements in plants
measurable_quantities: shape of the receptacle or axis
claims.candidate_data: Published 3D imaging of shoot apices and capitula (e.g. confocal datasets of Arabidopsis meristems) and floret coordinate datasets for sunflowers.

claims.label: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
claims.claim: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.
claims.quote: The spirals intersect isogonally, but orthogonal intersection would be only one particular case, and in all probability a very infrequent one, in the intersection of logarithmic spirals developed about a common pole.
claims.scope: parastichies in sunflower capitula and similar inflorescences
measurable_quantities: constancy of that angle across the disc
claims.candidate_data: Floret position datasets from sunflower seed-head images, such as the Turing's Sunflowers citizen-science dataset (Swinton et al. 2016).

claims.label: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals
claims.claim: There is no subtle mystery in phyllotaxis: the steady production of similar parts, similarly placed, at similar successive intervals of time necessarily produces symmetrical patterns (helices on a cylinder, logarithmic spirals on a surface containing the pole), which are a secondary mathematical result rather than a primary phenomenon.
claims.quote: I, for my part, see no subtle mystery in the matter, other than what lies in the steady production of similar growing parts, similarly situated, at similar successive intervals of time.
claims.scope: phyllotaxis of leaves, florets, bracts and scales
claims.candidate_data: Live-imaging datasets of shoot apical meristems with primordium timing and position (e.g. published Arabidopsis meristem time-lapse data).

claims.label: Parastichy counts on fir-cones are nearly constant within a species
claims.claim: The numbers of conspicuous parastichies on fir-cones are on the whole very constant within a species, e.g. 5 and 3 in the Norway spruce and 8 and 5 in the common larch.
claims.quote: and among fir-cones, we can easily count these, and we find them to be on the whole very constant in number, according to the species.
claims.scope: cones of conifers
measurable_quantities: number of parastichies in each direction per cone
claims.candidate_data: Published pine-cone and spruce-cone parastichy surveys and herbarium or museum cone collections.

claims.label: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
claims.claim: Phyllotactic parastichy numbers vary with the size of the whole structure, as in sunflower discs where one species may show 34/55, 55/89 or even 89/144 rows.
claims.quote: The arrangement, as we have seen, is apt to vary when the entire structure varies greatly in size, as in the disc of the sunflower.
claims.scope: sunflower capitula and other composite inflorescences
claims.candidate_data: Turing's Sunflowers citizen-science dataset of seed-head parastichy counts (Swinton et al. 2016).

claims.label: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
claims.claim: Within a species, cones with a given parastichy arrangement are nearly equally divided between right-handed and left-handed spiral directions (e.g. 224 versus 243 among 467 Norway spruce cones).
claims.quote: In each case they were nearly equally divided as regards direction; for instance of the 467 cones shewing the five-eight arrangement, the five-series ran in right-handed spirals in 224 cases, and in left-handed spirals in 243.
claims.scope: conifer cones (Norway spruce) and phyllotactic systems generally
claims.candidate_data: Published cone-chirality surveys and the Turing's Sunflowers dataset for capitulum chirality.

claims.label: One Fibonacci parastichy pair necessarily entails all the lower pairs
claims.claim: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.
claims.notation: F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1} (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots); pair (F_n, F_{n+1}) present \Rightarrow all lower pairs present
claims.quote: These are the very series which we have found to be common, or normal; and so far as our investigation has yet gone, it has proved to us that, if one of these exists, it entails, _ipso facto_, the presence of the rest.
claims.scope: spiral phyllotactic systems with a single genetic spiral
claims.candidate_data: Primordium coordinate datasets from cones, capitula and shoot apices.

claims.label: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
claims.claim: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.
claims.notation: t = 2 (more than two, fewer than three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral) \Rightarrow parastichy pairs from 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots; t = 3, 4, 5 give other series
claims.quote: And, determined in this manner, it is found in the great majority of cases, in fir-cones and a host of other examples of phyllotaxis, that _t_ = 2.
claims.scope: spiral phyllotaxis in plants
measurable_quantities: number of leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
claims.candidate_data: Published compilations of phyllotactic patterns across species and primordium position datasets from shoot apices.

claims.label: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
claims.claim: Which of the implicit spiral families is conspicuous does not depend on the angle of divergence but on the proportions of the leaves or scales, strictly on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area.
claims.notation: conspicuous parastichies set by the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area, not by the divergence angle
claims.quote: the conspicuousness of one set or another does not depend upon angular divergence. It depends on the relative proportions in length and breadth of the leaves themselves; or, more strictly speaking, on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboidal figure by which each leaf-area is circumscribed.
claims.scope: phyllotactic systems such as fir-cones
measurable_quantities: scale or leaf length and breadth
claims.candidate_data: Image datasets of conifer cones and capitula with scale dimensions and parastichy counts; none known as a combined dataset.

claims.section: Divergence angle and the golden mean
claims.label: Convergence of phyllotactic ratios to the golden mean has no biological significance
claims.claim: That the phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5… converge to 0.618…, the golden mean, is a mathematical coincidence without biological significance; the precise divergence angle and orthostichies are likewise unimportant.
claims.notation: \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{3}{5}, \tfrac{5}{8}, \dots \to (\sqrt{5} - 1)/2 \approx 0.618
claims.quote: And lastly, the fact that the successional numbers, expressed as fractions, 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, represent a convergent series, whose final term is equal to 0·61803..., the _sectio aurea_ or “golden mean” of unity, is seen to be a mathematical coincidence, devoid of biological significance
claims.scope: spiral phyllotaxis
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.section: Divergence angle and the golden mean
claims.label: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common
claims.claim: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.
claims.quote: the arrangements by which a better approximation is got, such as 8/13, 13/21, and the very close approximations such as 34/55, 55/89, 89/144, etc., are comparatively rare, while the much less close approximations of 3/5 or 2/3, or even 1/2, are extremely common.
claims.scope: phyllotaxis across plants
measurable_quantities: frequency of each phyllotactic fraction across species and organs
claims.candidate_data: Published cross-species compilations of phyllotactic fractions and the TRY plant trait database where leaf arrangement is recorded.

claims.section: Divergence angle and the golden mean
claims.label: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle
claims.claim: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.
claims.quote: then it is surely manifest that the simple way to do so is to elongate the axis, and to set the leaves further apart, lengthways on the stem. This has at once a far more potent effect than any nice manipulation of the “angle of divergence.”
claims.scope: leafy shoots of plants
claims.candidate_data: 3D plant architecture and light-interception modelling studies (e.g. functional–structural plant models) and TRY database shoot traits.

claims.section: Divergence angle and the golden mean
claims.label: The Fibonacci series has no adaptive role introduced by natural selection
claims.claim: The Fibonacci series in phyllotaxis, its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis that natural selection introduced it into plant structure have no place in the study of botanical phenomena.
claims.quote: We come then, without more ado, to the conclusion that the “Fibonacci series,” and its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis of its introduction into plant-structure through natural selection, are all matters which deserve no place in the plain study of botanical phenomena.
claims.scope: phyllotaxis in plants
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
claims.claim: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.
claims.quote: It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.
claims.scope: eggs of birds, tortoises and crocodiles
claims.candidate_data: The avian egg-shape dataset of Stoddard et al. (2017, Science) covering about 1,400 species; museum egg collections.

claims.label: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird
claims.claim: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.
claims.quote: It can be shown, at least as a very common rule, that those eggs which are most unsymmetrical, or most tapered off posteriorly, are also eggs of a large size relatively to the parent bird.
claims.scope: birds' eggs across species
claims.candidate_data: The Stoddard et al. (2017) avian egg-shape dataset with body mass from AVONET or EltonTraits.

claims.label: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones
claims.claim: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.
claims.quote: In the case of the common fowl we can trace a direct relation between the size and shape of the egg, for the first eggs laid by a young pullet are usually smaller, and at the same time are much more nearly spherical than the later ones
claims.scope: domestic fowl (Gallus gallus domesticus)
claims.candidate_data: Poultry science datasets on egg shape index versus hen age and breed.

claims.label: Peristaltic pressure behind the egg's middle makes the front blunt and rear pointed
claims.claim: Peristaltic contraction of the oviduct applies greatest pressure behind the middle of the forming egg, making the anterior end broader and the posterior narrower; the resulting tapered form also favours movement down the oviduct blunt end first.
claims.quote: from the nature and direction of motion of the peristaltic wave the pressure will be greatest somewhere behind the middle of the egg; in other words, the tube is converted for the time being into a more conical form, and the simple result follows that the anterior end of the egg becomes the broader and the posterior end the narrower.
claims.scope: birds' eggs
measurable_quantities: pressure distribution along the uterine wall
claims.candidate_data: Oviduct physiology and in vivo imaging studies of egg formation in poultry; none known as a dataset.

claims.label: Egg shape is caused by radial pressure of the oviduct before the shell hardens
claims.claim: The essential cause of the form and variation of form of an egg is the regularly varying, largely radial pressure applied by successive rings of the oviduct before the shell solidifies, not adaptation to nesting circumstances.
claims.quote: this factor, the unknown but regularly varying, largely radial, pressure applied by successive annuli of the oviduct, is the essential cause of the form, and variations of form, of the egg.
claims.scope: birds' eggs and other hard-shelled eggs
claims.candidate_data: The Stoddard et al. (2017) avian egg-shape dataset combined with oviduct physiology studies of the domestic fowl.

claims.label: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs
claims.claim: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.
claims.notation: p_n + T/r + T'/r' = P; with equal tensions p_n + T(1/r + 1/r') = P
claims.quote: In fact, in so far as the postulates correspond near enough to actualities, the above equation is the equation of _all eggs_ in the universe.
claims.scope: all hard-shelled and membrane-bound eggs
claims.candidate_data: The Stoddard et al. (2017) egg-shape dataset for curvature, with no known dataset of in-oviduct pressures.

claims.label: Membrane tension peaks at the small end, where abnormal eggs are irregular
claims.claim: In conical eggs with spherical ends, the tension of the envelope is greatest at and near the small end, so that is where eggs are most likely to be distorted or to burst and where abnormal eggs most often show irregularities.
claims.quote: further, that the tension _T_ is greatest at and near the small end of the egg. It is here, in short, that the egg is most likely to be irregularly distorted or even to burst, and it is here that we most commonly find irregularities of shape in abnormal eggs.
claims.scope: birds' eggs, especially pointed eggs and abnormal hen's eggs
measurable_quantities: location of shape irregularities on abnormal eggs
claims.candidate_data: Poultry science records of egg shell defects by location.

claims.label: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark
claims.claim: Following Looss, the lateral spine of some Schistosoma eggs is moulded mechanically in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus, so lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are mechanical variants of one thing and do not show the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni.
claims.quote: It ascribes to a mechanical cause a curious peculiarity of form; it shews, by reference to this mechanical principle, that two conditions which were very different to the systematic naturalist’s eye, were really only two simple mechanical modifications of the same thing; and it destroys the chief evidence for the existence of a supposed new species of worm
claims.scope: eggs of Schistosoma haematobium and S. mansoni
measurable_quantities: species identity of the adult worm producing them
claims.candidate_data: Schistosoma genome and molecular phylogeny data in GenBank and WormBase ParaSite, with egg morphology from parasitology collections.

claims.label: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity
claims.claim: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.
claims.quote: but we have no difficulty in seeing that the various forms represented in a series of sea-urchin shells are no other than those which we may easily and perfectly imitate in drops.
claims.scope: tests of regular echinoids
claims.candidate_data: 3D scans of echinoid tests on MorphoSource and the Natural History Museum's Echinoid Directory, compared with sessile-drop profiles.

claims.label: Vessel wall thickness tracks radius in large arteries but falls off in small ones
claims.claim: Under constant pressure the wall thickness of a blood-vessel should vary as its radius (P = T/R); because pressure falls with friction from large to small arteries, wall thickness is proportional to vessel size in larger vessels but becomes disproportionately thin in small arteries and capillaries.
claims.notation: P = T/R; at constant P, wall thickness t \propto R
claims.quote: and accordingly we find that while, for a time, the cross-sections of the larger and smaller vessels are symmetrical figures, with the wall-thickness proportional to the size of the tube, this proportion is gradually lost, and the walls of the small arteries, and still more of the capillaries, become exceedingly thin, and more so than in strict proportion to the narrowing of the tube.
claims.scope: arteries and capillaries of vertebrates
claims.candidate_data: Published vascular morphometry datasets of wall thickness and lumen diameter across the arterial tree, and blood pressure profiles.

claims.label: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber
claims.claim: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.
claims.notation: t(1/r + 1/r') = C within each cavity of the heart
claims.quote: that is to say, that the thickness (_t_) of the wall varies inversely as the mean curvature.
claims.scope: heart chambers of mammals
claims.candidate_data: Cardiac MRI datasets with wall thickness and curvature maps, such as UK Biobank cardiac imaging.

claims.label: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio
claims.claim: The left ventricle requires six to seven times the dilating pressure of the right, and its wall thickness is greater in the same proportion.
claims.notation: P_L/P_R \approx 6\text{--}7 \approx t_L/t_R
claims.quote: we find (1) that we have had to use a pressure in the left ventricle from six to seven times as great as in the right ventricle, and (2) that the thickness of the walls is just in the same proportion.
claims.scope: mammalian hearts
measurable_quantities: left and right ventricular wall thickness
claims.candidate_data: Cardiac MRI and echocardiography reference datasets (e.g. UK Biobank) and haemodynamic pressure records.

claims.label: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface
claims.claim: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).
claims.quote: The general principle is that the form and arrangement of the blood-vessels is such that the circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort, and with a minimum of wall-surface, the latter condition leading to a minimum of friction and being therefore included in the first.
claims.scope: vertebrate vascular systems
claims.candidate_data: Vascular network reconstructions from micro-CT and angiography datasets, analysed against minimum-work models.

claims.label: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles
claims.claim: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.
claims.quote: In other words, it would seem that for small branches a large angle of bifurcation, and for large branches a small one, is always the better.
claims.scope: arterial branching in vertebrates
claims.candidate_data: Vascular network reconstructions from micro-CT and angiography (e.g. published coronary and cerebral vessel tree datasets).

claims.label: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch
claims.claim: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).
claims.notation: \cos x = L/L', L and L' the energy loss per unit length in trunk and branch
claims.quote: That is to say, the most favourable angle of branching will be such that the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of the loss of energy which the blood undergoes, per unit of length, in the main vessel, as compared with that which it undergoes in the branch.
claims.scope: arterial branching in vertebrates
claims.candidate_data: Vascular network reconstructions with measured diameters and angles from micro-CT and angiography datasets.

claims.label: Mechanical adaptations of form are demonstrable, unlike colour adaptations
claims.claim: Unlike explanations of colouration as cryptic, warning or mimetic, which cannot be demonstrated, the fitness of organic form for mechanical functions such as swimming or flight can be analysed and established in detail by statics and dynamics.
claims.quote: But of a very different order from all such “adaptations” as these, are those very perfect adaptations of form which, for instance, fit a fish for swimming or a bird for flight. Here we are far above the region of mere hypothesis, for we have to deal with questions of mechanical efficiency where statical and dynamical considerations can be applied and established in detail.
claims.scope: adaptive form and colouration of animals in general
claims.candidate_data: none known

claims.label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
claims.claim: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.
claims.quote: At first sight, bone seems weak indeed; but it has the great and unusual advantage that it is very nearly as good for a tie as for a strut, nearly as strong to withstand rupture, or tearing asunder, as to resist crushing.
claims.scope: fresh (living) vertebrate bone
